stinging-nettle.habitat: Rich moist soil along streams, ditches, forest edges, and disturbed ground. Very common near Eugene waterways and coast range valleys toward Florence.
stinging-nettle.identification: Opposite serrated leaves with stinging hairs on stems and undersides. Square stems. Can reach 3–6 ft when flowering. Crushing or drying removes the sting.
lookalikes: White dead-nettle (Lamium album) — similar leaf shape but NO sting; square stem, white flowers.
Wood nettle (Laportea canadensis) — alternate leaves with sting; less common in Oregon.
Clearweed (Pilea pumila) — nettle-like but stingless and translucent stem.
stinging-nettle.edibleNotes: One of the most nutritious wild greens in the PNW. Young tops in spring taste like spinach. High in iron, calcium, and protein.
stinging-nettle.medicinalNotes: Traditional support for seasonal allergies, joint comfort, and nourishing tonics. Often used as dried leaf tea or tincture.
stinging-nettle.holisticNotes: A cornerstone “food as medicine” plant in Pacific Northwest herbalism — nutrient-dense and broadly tonifying.
stinging-nettle.preparation: Blanch or dry to neutralize sting. Tea, soup, pesto (blanched), or capsules from dried leaf.
stinging-nettle.harvestSeason: Young shoots: March–May. Handle with gloves.
safetyWarnings: Fresh stingers cause welts — always wear gloves when harvesting.
Avoid during pregnancy unless guided by a qualified herbalist.

oregon-grape.habitat: Dry to moist woodland understory throughout the Willamette Valley and coast range foothills.
oregon-grape.identification: Spiny holly-like evergreen leaflets in groups. Bright yellow flower clusters in early spring. Blue berries with whitish bloom in summer.
lookalikes: English holly (Ilex aquifolium) — invasive; red berries, not blue; alternate leaves on tree form.
Tall Oregon grape vs. dull Oregon grape (M. nervosa) — both edible berries; low ground cover vs. shrub.
Holly-leaved barberry — spiny but different flower and berry color.
oregon-grape.edibleNotes: Berries are very tart — best as jelly, syrup, or mixed with sweeter fruit. Not a snacking berry.
oregon-grape.medicinalNotes: Root and bark traditionally used as a bitter liver and digestive tonic. Contains berberine (similar action to goldenseal).
oregon-grape.holisticNotes: Oregon’s state flower and a signature “bitter tonic” in Western herbal practice.
oregon-grape.preparation: Berry: cook with sugar. Root: tincture or decoction (sustainably harvest only from abundant stands).
oregon-grape.harvestSeason: Flowers: Feb–Apr. Berries: Jul–Aug. Root: late fall.
safetyWarnings: Do not confuse with invasive English holly.
Berberine-containing plants may interact with medications — consult a practitioner.
Never strip roots from wild populations.

salmonberry.habitat: Stream banks, wetlands, and shady forest edges — abundant on the coast near Florence and in wet Willamette Valley corridors.
salmonberry.identification: Magenta flowers in spring. Compound leaves with three leaflets. Orange to red raspberry-like fruit.
lookalikes: Thimbleberry — soft red berry, huge maple-like leaves, no thorns.
Unripe Himalayan or trailing blackberry — black when ripe; salmonberry is orange-red.
Baneberry (Actaea) — white berries on thick stalk; TOXIC (rare in same habitat).
salmonberry.edibleNotes: Mild, slightly sweet-tart berries. Young shoots also peeled and eaten traditionally in spring.
salmonberry.medicinalNotes: Primarily food; berry antioxidants and seasonal nutrition.
salmonberry.holisticNotes: A reliable coast-range wild food — often one of the first berries of the season.
salmonberry.preparation: Eat fresh, jam, or dry. Young peeled shoots in spring.
safetyWarnings: Identify carefully vs. other Rubus species.

salal.habitat: Coastal conifer forest understory — dominant groundcover from Florence dunes inland and common in coast-range woods toward Eugene.
salal.identification: Leathery evergreen oval leaves. Urn-shaped pink-white flowers. Dark blue-purple mealy berries.
lookalikes: Evergreen huckleberry — similar dark berries but toothed leaves and grows as upright shrub, not groundcover.
Oregon grape berries — blue with bloom, very tart; compound holly-like leaves.
Nightshade (Solanum) berries — potentially toxic; salal has urn flowers and mealy texture.
salal.edibleNotes: Berries are sweet when fully ripe. Used in jams and pemmican traditionally.
salal.medicinalNotes: Leaf tea used as an astringent mouth rinse and mild anti-inflammatory wash.
salal.holisticNotes: Ubiquitous coast plant — berries are a staple wild food where salal thickets are dense.
salal.preparation: Berries fresh or dried. Leaf tea for topical or gargle use.
safetyWarnings: Leaves very astringent — don’t overconsume as tea.

miners-lettuce.habitat: Cool moist shady spots, woodland edges, and spring gardens throughout the valley.
miners-lettuce.identification: Succulent leaves with a cup-like leaf bracketing the flower stem. Small white or pink flowers.
lookalikes: Spring beauty (Claytonia sibirica) — pink flowers, no perfoliate disk; also edible.
Poison hemlock seedlings — NOT succulent; musty smell, hairless stems with purple blotches.
Chickweed — mat-forming, no cup leaf; also edible.
miners-lettuce.edibleNotes: Mild, crunchy salad green — entire aerial parts edible. Excellent source of vitamin C.
miners-lettuce.medicinalNotes: Historically used by miners to prevent scurvy.
miners-lettuce.holisticNotes: One of the easiest beginner wild foods in Western Oregon spring.
miners-lettuce.preparation: Raw in salads or lightly wilted.
safetyWarnings: Avoid areas sprayed with herbicides (roadsides).

yarrow.habitat: Meadows, roadsides, dry fields, and disturbed sunny ground valley-wide and along the coast highway corridor.
yarrow.identification: Feathery aromatic leaves. Flat-topped clusters of tiny white (sometimes pink) flowers. Distinct sage-like scent when crushed.
yarrow.medicinalNotes: Classic first-aid herb — styptic powder from dried leaves for minor cuts. Tea for fever support and digestion.
yarrow.holisticNotes: “Soldier’s woundwort” — one of the most widely used medicinal herbs in European and Indigenous traditions.
yarrow.preparation: Dried leaf and flower tea, poultice, or infused oil for topical use.
safetyWarnings: May cause contact dermatitis in sensitive people.
Avoid internal use in pregnancy.
Can potentiate sedatives in large doses.

plantain.habitat: Lawns, trails, compacted soil — everywhere in Eugene and Florence.
plantain.identification: Low rosette of ribbed oval leaves with parallel veins. Slender seed spikes rise from center.
plantain.medicinalNotes: Fresh leaf poultice for bee stings, bites, and splinters. Mucilage soothes skin and mucous membranes.
plantain.holisticNotes: A “footpath medicine” — often right underfoot on hikes near Spencer Butte or coastal trails.
plantain.preparation: Chew fresh leaf for poultice or dry for tea.
plantain.harvestSeason: Spring through fall; best before seed stalk hardens.
safetyWarnings: Ensure correct ID — not lily or other lookalikes.

dandelion.identification: Toothed basal leaves, hollow stem, yellow composite flower, white puffball seed head.
lookalikes: Cat’s-ear (Hypochaeris) — hairy leaves, solid stem, branching flower stalks.
Hawkweed (Hieracium) — similar yellow flowers but multiple blooms on branched stem.
False dandelion — always check for hollow stem and single flower per hollow stalk.
dandelion.edibleNotes: Young leaves in salad (bitter). Flowers for fritters. Roasted root as coffee substitute.
dandelion.medicinalNotes: Bitter root and leaf support digestion and liver function. Gentle diuretic (“piss-a-bed”).
dandelion.holisticNotes: Classic liver/spring tonic in Western herbalism.
dandelion.preparation: Salad greens, root decoction, flower wine.
safetyWarnings: Only harvest from unsprayed areas.
Latex may irritate skin.

red-clover.habitat: Meadows, pastures, and sunny fields in the Willamette Valley.
red-clover.identification: Three leaflets with pale chevron. Round pink-purple flower heads.
lookalikes: White clover (T. repens) — white flower heads; also edible.
Crown vetch — pink clusters on vine; NOT a true clover.
Alsike clover — pale pink; can cause toxicity in livestock (rare in humans).
red-clover.edibleNotes: Flower heads and young leaves in salads or tea.
red-clover.medicinalNotes: Traditional support for skin health and menopausal comfort. Contains isoflavones.
red-clover.preparation: Dried blossom tea or fresh in salads.
safetyWarnings: May affect hormone-sensitive conditions — consult practitioner.

elderberry.habitat: Stream banks, open woods, and disturbed sunny edges in the valley.
elderberry.identification: Opposite compound leaves. Large flat cream flower clusters. Powdery blue berries on reddish stems.
lookalikes: Red elderberry (S. racemosa) — red berry clusters on coast; TOXIC raw.
Blue elder vs. red elder — blue powdery berries vs. upright red clusters.
Hercules’ club / devil’s walking stick — similar flower shape but armed stems; berries different.
elderberry.edibleNotes: Berries must be cooked — used for syrup, jam, and wine.
elderberry.medicinalNotes: Cooked berry syrup traditionally used for immune support during cold season.
elderberry.holisticNotes: One of the most popular home herbal preparations in North America.
elderberry.preparation: Cook berries at least 20 minutes. Strain seeds. Syrup with honey.
safetyWarnings: NEVER eat raw berries — nausea and worse.
Red elderberry (S. racemosa) on coast is toxic — learn the difference.
Leaves, bark, and seeds are toxic.

fireweed.habitat: Burn sites, roadsides, clearcuts, and open meadows — common coast to cascades.
fireweed.identification: Tall spikes of magenta four-petaled flowers. Long narrow leaves. Fluffy seed parachutes.
lookalikes: Foxglove (Digitalis) — tall spike; TOXIC. Leaves wider, flowers tubular spotted.
Purple loosestrife — invasive wetland spike; different leaf arrangement.
Fireweed has 4 petals; many lookalikes have different flower counts.
fireweed.edibleNotes: Young shoots peeled like asparagus. Leaves as cooked green. Honey from fireweed is prized.
fireweed.medicinalNotes: Mucilaginous — soothing for irritated GI tract. Traditional anti-inflammatory.
fireweed.holisticNotes: Pioneer species that heals disturbed land — symbolic in PNW ecology.
fireweed.preparation: Peel young shoots; leaf tea; flower blossom garnish.
safetyWarnings: Positive ID vs. other tall magenta spikes.

licorice-fern.habitat: Mossy tree trunks, rocks, and wet forest — very common in coast range and valley forests.
licorice-fern.identification: Fronds from creeping rhizome on mossy maples and logs. Sweet licorice-scented rhizome when chewed.
licorice-fern.medicinalNotes: Rhizome traditionally chewed for sore throat and cough — demulcent and sweet.
licorice-fern.holisticNotes: Look up on big leaf maple trunks on hikes between Eugene and the coast.
licorice-fern.preparation: Fresh or dried rhizome tea; chew small piece for throat.
licorice-fern.harvestSeason: Year-round rhizome; take only small portions sustainably.
safetyWarnings: Overharvest damages host ecosystem — take sparingly.

redwood-sorrel.habitat: Shady moist conifer forest floor — coast range and old growth near Florence.
redwood-sorrel.identification: Three heart-shaped leaflets often folded. White to pink five-petaled flowers. Sour lemon taste.
lookalikes: Wood sorrel vs. clover — sorrel has heart-shaped leaflets in threes; clover has oval leaflets with chevron.
Violet leaves — similar heart shape but no sour taste; different flowers.
Redwood sorrel is Oxalis; do not confuse with shamrock clover for large harvests.
redwood-sorrel.edibleNotes: Small amounts as trail nibble — oxalic acid gives sour flavor.
redwood-sorrel.holisticNotes: Beautiful forest floor indicator species in coast range hikes.
redwood-sorrel.preparation: Few leaves fresh — not large quantities.
safetyWarnings: High oxalates — avoid large amounts; kidney stone risk.
Do not confuse with clover.

huckleberry.habitat: Coastal and low-elevation forest understory — Florence dunes forest and coast range.
huckleberry.identification: Leathery serrated evergreen leaves. Pink urn flowers. Dark purple-black sweet berries.
lookalikes: Salal — groundcover with similar dark berries; leathery entire leaves without serrations.
Baldhip rose hips — red, not purple-black berries.
Nightshade berries — grow in different plant form; always confirm serrated evergreen leaves.
huckleberry.edibleNotes: Excellent wild berry — fresh, jam, pancakes. Ripen further after picking.
huckleberry.holisticNotes: Coast range counterpart to valley black huckleberry species.
safetyWarnings: Positive berry ID essential.

cottonwood.habitat: River bottoms and wet lowland — Willamette River corridor and coastal river valleys.
cottonwood.identification: Large cottonwood with balsam-scented sticky buds in late winter. Heart-shaped toothed leaves.
cottonwood.medicinalNotes: Balm of Gilead — cottonwood buds infused in oil for salves on sore muscles and skin irritation.
cottonwood.holisticNotes: Late winter bud harvest is a traditional PNW herbalist ritual along the Willamette.
cottonwood.preparation: Collect fuzzy buds before leaf-out. Infuse in olive oil 4–6 weeks. Strain for salve.
safetyWarnings: Tree identification only — do not girdle trees.

willow.habitat: Wetlands, stream banks, and lakeshores — common in Eugene wetlands and coastal estuaries near Florence.
willow.identification: Flexible branches. Long narrow leaves often with silky undersides. Catkins in early spring.
willow.medicinalNotes: Bark contains salicin (aspirin precursor). Traditional tea for pain and fever — bitter.
willow.holisticNotes: The original “aspirin plant” — use with respect and medical awareness.
willow.preparation: Bark tea from pruned twigs only — never ring-bark living trees.
willow.harvestSeason: Bark: early spring on pruned material.
safetyWarnings: Avoid if allergic to aspirin.
Not for children with viral illness (Reye syndrome risk with salicylates).
Can interact with blood thinners.

self-heal.identification: Low plant with square stem. Purple tubular flowers in dense head. Lance-shaped leaves.
self-heal.medicinalNotes: Traditional wound herb and throat-soothing tea. Mild antimicrobial reputation.
self-heal.holisticNotes: Name says it all — common “lawyer’s woundwort” of European herbalism, naturalized in Oregon.
safetyWarnings: Generally mild — verify ID.

cleavers.habitat: Moist shady edges, gardens, and stream banks.
cleavers.identification: Square stem with whorled narrow leaves that cling (hooked hairs). Tiny white flowers.
cleavers.medicinalNotes: Spring lymphatic tonic — fresh juice or tea. Traditional diuretic and skin support.
cleavers.holisticNotes: Best used fresh in spring cleanse protocols in Western herbal tradition.
cleavers.preparation: Cold infusion of fresh plant or juiced tops.
safetyWarnings: Diuretic — hydrate well. Avoid if pregnant.

usnea.habitat: Hanging from tree branches in moist clean air — coast range and valley forests after rain.
usnea.identification: Gray-green branched lichen with white elastic cord inside main stem when pulled apart.
usnea.medicinalNotes: Traditional antimicrobial for respiratory and urinary support. Usnic acid content.
usnea.holisticNotes: Harvest only from fallen branches after storms — sustainable practice.
usnea.preparation: Alcohol tincture or hot water decoction (strain well).
safetyWarnings: Liver toxicity possible with prolonged high-dose usnic acid — short-term use only.
Never harvest from polluted areas.

turkey-tail.habitat: Dead hardwood and conifer logs — everywhere in Oregon forests.
turkey-tail.identification: Bracket fungus with concentric color bands. Underside white with tiny pores (not gills).
turkey-tail.medicinalNotes: Immune-modulating polysaccharides (PSK/PSP) — studied extensively in Asia. Long decoction.
turkey-tail.holisticNotes: One of the safest and most researched medicinal mushrooms for daily broth.
turkey-tail.preparation: Slow simmer 1–4 hours for broth or dual-extract tincture.
safetyWarnings: Must be pore surface — not gilled mushrooms.
Wild mushroom ID confidence required.

chanterelle.habitat: Mossy conifer forest floor — coast range and valley foothills after fall rains.
chanterelle.identification: Golden funnel-shaped cap with false gills (forked ridges). Fruity apricot smell. No true gills.
lookalikes: Jack-o-lantern (Omphalotus) — grows in clusters on wood; TRUE gills; ORANGE bioluminescent; causes severe GI illness.
False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca) — true thin gills, softer flesh, no apricot scent.
Woolly chanterelle (Turbinellus floccosus) — vase-shaped with woolly cap; causes GI upset for many.
chanterelle.edibleNotes: Oregon state mushroom. Premier wild edible — sauté, dry, freeze.
chanterelle.holisticNotes: Fall mushroom hunting is a PNW tradition from Eugene foothills to coast range near Florence.
chanterelle.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Never eat raw wild mushrooms.
safetyWarnings: DEADLY lookalike: Jack-o-lantern (Omphalotus) — learn false gills vs. true gills.
Always confirm with experienced forager first season.

beach-strawberry.habitat: Coastal sand dunes and bluffs — Florence to Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area.
beach-strawberry.identification: Three toothed leaflets, runners on sand. Small sweet white-flowered berries close to ground.
lookalikes: Wild strawberry (F. virginiana) — inland; similar but often in forest edges not dunes.
Mock strawberry (Duchesnea) — yellow flowers, bland/hollow berry; not sweet.
Cinquefoil — five leaflets, yellow flowers; not a true strawberry.
beach-strawberry.edibleNotes: Tiny intense strawberries — best trail snack on dune walks.
beach-strawberry.holisticNotes: Coast-specific wild food not found inland in Eugene.
safetyWarnings: Stay on trails in dune habitat — fragile ecosystem.

douglas-fir-tip.habitat: Dominant conifer from valley floor to coast — everywhere.
douglas-fir-tip.identification: Soft bright green new growth tips in spring. Distinct bracts on cones (“mouse tail and legs”).
lookalikes: Western yew (Taxus brevifolia) — TOXIC; flat dark green needles, red cup berry, no pine-like cones.
Spruce/hemlock tips — edible in tea but different needle arrangement and cone type.
Only harvest from true Douglas fir with the three-pronged bracts on cones.
douglas-fir-tip.edibleNotes: Citrus-pine flavored tips for tea, syrup, and seasoning. High vitamin C.
douglas-fir-tip.medicinalNotes: Resinous tea for congestion. Traditional respiratory support.
douglas-fir-tip.holisticNotes: Signature tree of the PNW — spring tip harvest connects you to forest seasonality.
douglas-fir-tip.preparation: Tea, infused honey, or dried for winter.
safetyWarnings: Avoid yew (toxic) — flat needles, red cup on berry.

nootka-rose.habitat: Stream banks, roadsides, and open sunny areas valley and coast.
nootka-rose.identification: Pink five-petaled flowers. Thorns on stems. Large red rose hips in fall.
lookalikes: Baldhip rose (R. gymnocarpa) — hips lose sepals early; also edible with same hair caution.
Himalayan blackberry — thorny but compound leaves and aggregate fruit, not rose hips.
Any rose hip has irritating hairs inside — strain all preparations.
nootka-rose.edibleNotes: Rose hips extremely high in vitamin C — tea and jelly. Petals for garnish.
nootka-rose.medicinalNotes: Astringent hip tea for digestive and skin support.
nootka-rose.holisticNotes: Fall hip harvest along Willamette paths and coastal trails.
nootka-rose.preparation: Remove seeds/hairs from hips before eating. Tea or syrup.
nootka-rose.harvestSeason: Flowers: May–Jun. Hips: after first frost.
safetyWarnings: Irritating hairs inside hips — strain well.

horsetail.habitat: Sandy wet soils, roadsides, and disturbed ground.
horsetail.identification: Jointed hollow stems with whorled branches. Silica-rich. Two stages: fertile brown cone stage and green vegetative.
horsetail.medicinalNotes: High silica — traditional use for hair, skin, nails, and connective tissue support.
horsetail.holisticNotes: Ancient plant lineage — use short-term only in modern herbal practice.
horsetail.preparation: Long decoction of dried sterile stems. Never raw.
safetyWarnings: Contains thiaminase — long-term use may deplete B1.
Avoid in pregnancy and with alcoholism.
Contains nicotine — not for children.

thimbleberry.habitat: Openings, stream banks, and forest edges from Willamette Valley foothills to coast range near Florence. Large soft maple-like leaves on thornless stems.
thimbleberry.identification: Huge velvety 5-lobed maple-shaped leaves. White flowers in spring. Bright red soft berries that pull off like a thimble. No thorns.
lookalikes: Salmonberry — orange to red berry, magenta flowers, three leaflets (not maple-shaped).
Himalayan blackberry — thorny canes; hard black fruit, not soft thimble.
Baneberry — white toxic berries on thick stalk; completely different leaf shape.
thimbleberry.edibleNotes: One of the best fresh-eating trail berries in the PNW — soft, tart-sweet, doesn’t ship so you rarely see it in stores. Jam and sauce within hours of picking.
thimbleberry.holisticNotes: Classic coast-to-valley summer berry — often growing with salmonberry on the same hike.
thimbleberry.preparation: Eat fresh, freezer jam, or cook into sauce. Too delicate to dry well.
thimbleberry.harvestSeason: Berries: July–August. Young shoots peeled in spring (traditional).
safetyWarnings: Positive Rubus ID — no thorns distinguishes from blackberries.

trailing-blackberry.habitat: Sunny roadsides, clearings, and dry edges throughout Lane County and coastal scrub toward Florence. Low trailing vines, not tall canes.
trailing-blackberry.identification: Thin trailing stems with small hooked prickles. White to pink flowers. Small intense black berries with excellent flavor — parent of many cultivated varieties.
lookalikes: Himalayan blackberry — tall arching canes, larger berries; also edible but invasive.
Dewberry — similar trailing habit; confirm 5-part leaves and Rubus ID.
Nightshade berries — NOT on thorny Rubus stems; always check flower structure.
trailing-blackberry.edibleNotes: Oregon’s native wild blackberry — smaller but far more aromatic than Himalayan blackberry. Best pies and jam berry in the valley.
trailing-blackberry.holisticNotes: Seek out native patches instead of invasive Himalaya thickets when possible.
trailing-blackberry.preparation: Fresh, pie, jam, vinegar, or freeze on sheet trays.
safetyWarnings: Do not confuse with unripe or toxic berries on other plants.
Himalayan blackberry is invasive but also edible — native trailing has finer flavor.

red-huckleberry.habitat: Often on decaying logs and stumps in moist conifer forest — common in coast range hikes near Florence and foothill forests around Eugene.
red-huckleberry.identification: Tiny bright green leaves on angular green stems. Small red translucent berries. Grows on wood, not in soil (key ID clue).
lookalikes: Evergreen huckleberry — dark berries on woody shrub in soil, not from logs.
Salal — dark blue mealy berries, leathery oval leaves.
Red berries on green stems from wood is the key — do not pick bush berries by mistake.
red-huckleberry.edibleNotes: Tart bright berries — outstanding for pancakes, muffins, and syrup. Less sweet than evergreen huckleberry but incredible baked.
red-huckleberry.holisticNotes: Look for red berries on green stems sprouting from old logs.
red-huckleberry.preparation: Cook with sugar, bake, or dry for winter tea. Raw is quite tart.
safetyWarnings: Some Vaccinium species look similar — confirm red berries on woody stems from logs.

serviceberry.habitat: Open slopes, oak savanna edges, and sunny forest margins in the eastern Willamette Valley and foothills — less common on immediate coast but present inland.
serviceberry.identification: Shrub or small tree. White spring flowers in clusters. Blue-purple berries with crown scar on bottom (like tiny apples). Oval finely toothed leaves.
lookalikes: Blue elderberry — cluster berries without crown scar on each fruit; opposite leaves.
Huckleberries — single berries, no crown scar dimple.
Nightshade — may have berry clusters; lacks apple-like crown scar on each fruit.
serviceberry.edibleNotes: Sweet nutty berries — excellent fresh, in pies, or dried like raisins. One of the best “fruit tree” wild foods in eastern Lane County.
serviceberry.holisticNotes: Ripens early — often called Juneberry for a reason.
serviceberry.preparation: Fresh, pie, fruit leather, or dry. Remove stems.
safetyWarnings: Berries must have crown scar (bottom dimple) like blueberry — not a nightshade.

chickweed.habitat: Cool moist gardens, farm edges, and disturbed soil — abundant in Eugene valley winter and spring; mild coast winters near Florence.
chickweed.identification: Low tangled mat. Opposite oval leaves. Tiny white star flowers with five deeply split petals (looks like ten). Single line of hairs on stem that switches sides at each node.
lookalikes: Mouse-ear chickweed — similar; also edible.
Spurge (Euphorbia) — milky sap when broken; NOT edible — TOXIC.
Scarlet pimpernel — low mat; different flower color; not edible.
chickweed.edibleNotes: Mild salad green — tastes like corn silk or mild lettuce. High in vitamins. One of the best winter wild greens in the valley.
chickweed.holisticNotes: Harvest when lush and green — bolts and fades in hot dry summer.
chickweed.preparation: Raw in salads, pesto, or brief wilt in soup. Do not cook long.
chickweed.harvestSeason: Best: October–April. Fades in summer heat.
safetyWarnings: Learn the stem-hair ID — spurge and other lookalikes lack the hair line.
Wash well — often grows near foot traffic.

lambs-quarters.habitat: Disturbed soil, gardens, and farm fields throughout Eugene and coastal towns — classic “weed” superfood.
lambs-quarters.identification: Gray-green leaves often with mealy white coating on undersides. Diamond toothed shape. Tall spikes of tiny green flowers in summer.
lookalikes: Orach (Atriplex) — related edible; similar leaf shape.
Nightshade (Solanum) — may resemble young shoots; TOXIC berries and leaves.
Spinach — cultivated lookalike; wild lambs quarters has mealy coating under leaves.
lambs-quarters.edibleNotes: Top wild spinach substitute — steam, sauté, or blend in smoothies. More nutritious than cultivated spinach by many measures.
lambs-quarters.holisticNotes: Young plants are tender; pinch tops for continued harvest.
lambs-quarters.preparation: Steam or sauté young leaves and tips. Blanch and freeze for winter.
lambs-quarters.harvestSeason: Young leaves: spring–early summer before flowering.
safetyWarnings: Always cook or blanch — raw in large amounts contains oxalates.
Avoid plants from contaminated soil (lead, pesticides).

wild-mint.habitat: Wet meadows, ditches, and stream margins — Willamette valley waterways and coastal creek bottoms near Florence.
wild-mint.identification: Square stems. Opposite toothed leaves. Strong mint smell when crushed. Whorls of small lavender flowers.
lookalikes: Horse mint / other Mentha — must smell strongly of mint when crushed.
Ground ivy (Glechoma) — mint family but creeping; different flower shape.
Pennyroyal — mint family; historically used but toxic in large doses.
wild-mint.edibleNotes: Tea, tabbouleh, fruit salads, and syrup. Classic digestive and cooling summer herb.
wild-mint.holisticNotes: Crush a leaf — if it doesn’t smell minty, it’s not mint.
wild-mint.preparation: Fresh or dried tea. Infused honey. Chop leaves into salads.
wild-mint.harvestSeason: Spring through fall — best before flowering for tenderest leaves.
safetyWarnings: Must smell strongly of mint — toxic lookalikes exist without mint odor.
Avoid polluted ditches.

cattail.habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, ponds, and slow sloughs — West Eugene wetlands, Fern Ridge area, and Siuslaw estuary margins.
cattail.identification: Tall sword-like leaves. Brown hot-dog seed heads in late summer. Grows in standing water or saturated mud.
lookalikes: Iris (blue flag) — TOXIC; flat fan of leaves, showy flowers, no brown cigar head.
Sweet flag (Acorus) — similar wetland leaves; different flower spike; check habitat.
Prairie cordgrass — sharp edges; not the classic cattail cigar seed head.
cattail.edibleNotes: Four-season food: spring white shoots (peel), early green flower spikes (corn-on-the-cob), pollen flour, and starchy rhizomes in fall/winter.
cattail.holisticNotes: The “supermarket of the swamp” — learn one plant for many calories.
cattail.preparation: Peel young shoots for stir-fry. Boil immature green spikes 5 min. Pollen in baked goods. Rhizome starch requires cleaning.
cattail.harvestSeason: Shoots: spring. Pollen: early summer. Roots: fall.
safetyWarnings: NEVER harvest where water may be contaminated (ag runoff, sewage).
Do not confuse with toxic iris (flat fan leaves, no cattail seed head).

pacific-crabapple.habitat: Wet coastal forest and stream banks — native from Florence estuary north; occasional in valley riparian plantings.
pacific-crabapple.identification: Small tree with thorny twigs. White to pink spring blossoms. Yellow to reddish crabapples under 1 inch — very tart raw.
lookalikes: Cultivated apple escapes — larger fruit; similar but often bigger leaves.
Hawthorn (Crataegus) — similar rosaceous fruit; hawthorn berries have different seed pattern.
Chokecherry — dark purple-black drupes in racemes, not small apples.
pacific-crabapple.edibleNotes: Classic pectin-rich wild fruit for jelly and cider. High natural pectin means excellent set without added box pectin.
pacific-crabapple.holisticNotes: Coast specialty — combine with sweeter fruit for sauce.
pacific-crabapple.preparation: Cook and strain for jelly. Cider vinegar. Never eat large amounts raw.
pacific-crabapple.harvestSeason: Fruit: September–October after frost sweetens slightly.
safetyWarnings: Very tart raw — cook before eating in quantity.
Crush seeds contain amygdalin — don’t eat crushed seeds.

morel.habitat: Burn scars, disturbed soil, cottonwood bottoms, and old orchards in the Willamette Valley — spring specialty after warm rains.
morel.identification: Honeycombed pitted cap attached to stem. Hollow inside entire mushroom (cut lengthwise to verify). No gills — pits and ridges.
lookalikes: False morel (Gyromitra) — brain-like red-brown cap; NOT fully hollow; contains gyromitrin — TOXIC.
Verpa (thimble cap) — cap attached only at top of stem; cap separates from stalk.
Stinkhorn eggs — may resemble young morels; break open to check for developing stalk smell.
morel.edibleNotes: Premier spring gourmet mushroom — sauté in butter, dry for year-round use. Oregon spring morel season rivals anywhere in North America.
morel.holisticNotes: Check burn permits and land access — popular on public land near Eugene foothills.
morel.preparation: Always cook thoroughly. Split and wash out grit. Dry or sauté — never raw.
morel.harvestSeason: March–May after soil reaches ~50°F and spring rains.
safetyWarnings: MUST be hollow — false morels (Gyromitra) are solid and toxic.
Never eat raw — cook every wild mushroom.
Know land rules — some areas restrict mushroom harvest.

purslane.habitat: Hot dry disturbed soil — garden paths, farm rows, and sandy lots in Eugene summer and Florence coastal gardens.
purslane.identification: Succulent red stems sprawling on ground. Small fleshy oval leaves. Tiny yellow flowers. Leaves feel juicy when pinched.
lookalikes: Spurge (Euphorbia) — milky white sap when stem broken; NOT succulent — TOXIC.
Spotted spurge — prostrate; exudes milky latex.
Purslane has no milky sap — that is the critical field test.
purslane.edibleNotes: Highest plant source of omega-3 ALA among common weeds. Tangy lemon crunch in salads and tacos.
purslane.holisticNotes: Thrives in summer heat when other greens bolt — valuable dry-season food.
purslane.preparation: Raw in salads, pickled stems, or brief sauté. Thickens soups.
safetyWarnings: Do not confuse with spurge — spurge has milky sap and is NOT succulent.
Wash away soil — low-growing.

burdock.habitat: Disturbed ground, trailsides, and vacant lots — ubiquitous weed with Velcro-like seed heads.
burdock.identification: Large heart-shaped leaves with woolly undersides. Purple thistle-like flowers. Round bur seed heads that stick to clothing.
lookalikes: Rhubarb — cultivated; similar large leaves but no burs; poisonous leaves on rhubarb too.
Butterbur (Petasites) — huge leaves; different flower timing; not the same root.
Foxglove first-year rosette — TOXIC; soft fuzzy leaves but different venation.
burdock.edibleNotes: First-year roots are the famous Japanese gobo — earthy, crunchy, stir-fry staple. Peel thick skin; soak to reduce bitterness.
burdock.holisticNotes: Harvest roots first fall or spring from first-year rosettes (no flower stalk yet).
burdock.preparation: Scrub, peel, slice, soak 30 min. Stir-fry, pickle, or add to miso soup. Young leaf petioles peeled.
burdock.harvestSeason: Roots: fall or spring of first year. Stalks: before flowers open.
safetyWarnings: Only first-year plants — woody second-year roots are inedible.
Flower stalk appears second year — then root is too tough.

wild-lettuce.habitat: Roadsides, vacant lots, farm edges, and disturbed soil throughout Eugene and the Willamette Valley — also along I-5 corridor toward Florence. Tall weed with milky sap.
wild-lettuce.identification: L. serriola: prickly spines on midrib underside, blue-green leaves, tall flowering stalk with small yellow dandelion-like flowers. L. virosa: larger, more robust cousin with similar milky latex. Both bleed white sap when stem is broken.
wild-lettuce.medicinalNotes: Folk “lettuce opium” lore — dried latex (lactucarium) historically used for pain and sleep in 19th-century herbalism. Modern evidence is weak; effects are mild compared to true opiates.
wild-lettuce.holisticNotes: Common valley weed — often confused with sow thistle. The sap is the traditional focus, not the leaves as salad.
wild-lettuce.preparation: Historical: score stem, collect dried white sap. Modern herbalism sometimes uses tincture of flowering tops. Educational reference only.
wild-lettuce.harvestSeason: Flowering stalks: summer. Sap: when stems are actively growing.
safetyWarnings: Not a substitute for prescribed pain medication.
Can cause drowsiness — do not drive or combine with sedatives.
L. virosa is more potent in folklore; positive species ID required.
Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

pokeweed.habitat: Disturbed ground, fence lines, and garden edges — naturalized in parts of western Oregon including Willamette Valley towns. Less common on immediate coast but reported inland from Florence.
pokeweed.identification: Large herbaceous perennial with red-purple stems. Alternate oval leaves. Long drooping racemes of white flowers followed by dark purple-black berries on hot pink pedicels.
pokeweed.medicinalNotes: Traditional Southern and Appalachian folk medicine — berries and roots appear in “detox” and immune folklore. All parts contain saponins and lectins (especially root and seeds).
pokeweed.holisticNotes: Young spring shoots were historically boiled in multiple changes of water (“poke sallet”) — a dangerous practice if done incorrectly.
pokeweed.preparation: Historical reference only. Modern herbalism does not recommend internal use. Topical applications appear in some folk traditions.
pokeweed.harvestSeason: Spring shoots (historical only) — berries ripen late summer.
safetyWarnings: ROOTS AND SEEDS ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — can cause severe vomiting, diarrhea, and death.
Raw berries poisonous to children and pets.
Do not follow social-media “detox” protocols.
If ingested, call Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 immediately.

comfrey.habitat: Garden escape and riparian edges — widely planted in Eugene valley herb gardens and naturalized near streams. Large hairy leaves in basal rosette.
comfrey.identification: Coarse hairy lance-shaped leaves with decurrent wings on stem. Clusters of drooping bell-shaped purple to cream flowers. Thick black taproot.
comfrey.medicinalNotes: Allantoin-rich leaves traditionally used for bruises, sprains, and topical wound support. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) in roots and leaves damage the liver when taken internally.
comfrey.holisticNotes: FDA and European regulators have restricted or banned oral comfrey products — yet it remains one of the most popular folk topical herbs in Pacific Northwest homestead culture.
comfrey.preparation: External only: infused oil or poultice from dried leaves. Never use on broken skin long-term. Do not ingest teas, capsules, or tinctures.
comfrey.harvestSeason: Leaves: before flowering (spring). Flowers: early summer.
safetyWarnings: BANNED for internal use in many countries — hepatotoxic PAs accumulate.
Do not use during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Do not apply open-wound poultices without qualified herbalist guidance.
Russian comfrey (S. × uplandicum) is also PA-containing.

sheep-sorrel.habitat: Lawns, pastures, roadsides, and disturbed acidic soils — one of the most common weeds in Oregon. Often grows alongside burdock in the same disturbed patches.
sheep-sorrel.identification: Arrowhead-shaped leaves with basal lobes pointing backward (sheep’s head silhouette). Red-tinged stems. Small reddish flower spikes on wire-like stalks. Sour lemon taste from oxalic acid.
sheep-sorrel.medicinalNotes: Key ingredient in the Essiac folk cancer-support tea formula (with burdock root, slippery elm, and Indian rhubarb). No clinical proof of anti-cancer effect; used historically as cooling astringent.
sheep-sorrel.holisticNotes: Pairs ecologically and in herbal lore with burdock — both common valley “weeds” with deep folk followings.
sheep-sorrel.preparation: Essiac-style decoctions use dried aerial parts. Small amounts in salad. Tea from dried herb.
sheep-sorrel.harvestSeason: Spring through summer before seed set.
safetyWarnings: High oxalates — avoid large amounts; kidney stone risk.
Essiac and cancer claims are not FDA-approved — consult oncology providers.
Do not confuse with toxic lookalikes in unrelated families.

psilocybe-cyanescens.habitat: Wood-chip mulch, landscaped beds, trail edges, and decaying hardwood debris — extremely common in urban Eugene and coastal towns like Florence after fall rains.
psilocybe-cyanescens.identification: Caramel to chestnut cap with wavy margin when mature. White stem bruises blue-green. Purple-brown spore print. Grows in clusters on wood chips — not on open pasture.
psilocybe-cyanescens.holisticNotes: One of the most frequently encountered psilocybin mushrooms in the Pacific Northwest. Documented on iNaturalist throughout Lane County.
psilocybe-cyanescens.harvestSeason: Late fall through winter after first heavy rains (Oct–Jan).
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL to possess in Oregon except within approved psilocybin service contexts — know state and federal law.
Deadly lookalikes exist — Galerina marginata grows on wood and contains amatoxins.
Misidentification can be fatal. Never eat wild mushrooms without expert confirmation.
Educational reference only — not medical or legal advice.

psilocybe-azurescens.habitat: Coastal Oregon wood chips, dune grasses, and sandy soils with woody debris — first described near the Oregon coast. Reported from Florence north toward Astoria.
psilocybe-azurescens.identification: Large caramel cap (can exceed 10 cm). Robust stem with blue bruising. Often grows in coastal wood-chip piles and edge habitats.
psilocybe-azurescens.holisticNotes: Oregon coast endemic species — a signature mushroom of Pacific Northwest mycology.
psilocybe-azurescens.harvestSeason: Late fall (Nov–Dec) on the coast after rains.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed Oregon psilocybin services.
Potent — dosage errors are dangerous even with correct ID.
Wood-chip patches may contain toxic Galerina species.
Educational reference only.

psilocybe-semilanceata.habitat: Sheep and cattle pastures, lawns, and fertilized grass in cool wet weather — reported in Willamette Valley pastures.
psilocybe-semilanceata.identification: Small conical bell-shaped cap with pointed papilla. Thin wavy stem. Purple-brown spore print. Grows from grass, not wood.
psilocybe-semilanceata.holisticNotes: Classic European pasture species also found in Pacific Northwest grasslands.
psilocybe-semilanceata.harvestSeason: Fall through early winter during cool wet spells.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed contexts.
Easily confused with toxic lawn mushrooms.
Never harvest on grazed pastures without landowner permission.

psilocybe-allenii.habitat: Wood-chip mulch and landscaped beds along the Oregon coast and I-5 corridor — first described from the San Francisco Bay Area and documented north into coastal Oregon towns including the Florence area.
psilocybe-allenii.identification: Caramel to chestnut cap, often wavy when mature. White stem with strong blue bruising. Purple-brown spore print. Grows on wood chips — member of the Pacific wood-lover complex related to P. cyanescens.
psilocybe-allenii.holisticNotes: Often found alongside P. cyanescens in the same mulch beds — cap size and subtle macro features help separate species.
psilocybe-allenii.harvestSeason: Late fall through winter (Nov–Jan) after rains.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed Oregon psilocybin service contexts.
Deadly Galerina marginata shares the same wood-chip habitat.
Spore print and expert confirmation mandatory.
Educational reference only.

psilocybe-stuntzii.habitat: Lawns, grassy areas near conifers, and mulched beds in the Willamette Valley — named for UW mycologist Daniel Stuntz. Common in Eugene-area campus lawns and park edges after fall rains.
psilocybe-stuntzii.identification: Small to medium brown cap. Stem bruises blue-green distinctly (“blue legs”). Purple-brown spore print. Often grows in grass or near wood chips — not a large wood-cluster species.
psilocybe-stuntzii.holisticNotes: One of the classic PNW lawn-and-mulch psilocybes — smaller than cyanescens but similarly potent.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed contexts.
Lawn mushrooms include toxic species — never rely on blue bruising alone.
Pesticide-treated lawns are unsafe to forage.
Educational reference only.

psilocybe-baeocystis.habitat: Mulched garden beds, bark chips, and rich soil under conifers — reported throughout western Oregon from valley cities to coast range towns near Florence.
psilocybe-baeocystis.identification: Dark olive-brown conical cap (“bottle cap” shape). Stem often banded and bruises blue. Distinctive baeocystin content in chemistry literature. Purple-brown spore print.
psilocybe-baeocystis.holisticNotes: Named for the bottle-cap silhouette of young specimens — another cyanescens-complex wood-lover.
psilocybe-baeocystis.harvestSeason: Late fall through winter on mulched beds.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed contexts.
Galerina and other wood-inhabiting amatoxin species are deadly lookalikes.
Educational reference only — not medical or legal advice.

gymnopilus-spectabilis.habitat: Large clusters on conifer stumps and logs throughout Oregon forests — valley foothills and coast range near Florence.
gymnopilus-spectabilis.identification: Big orange-brown caps in dense clusters on wood. Rusty orange spore print (not purple-brown). Often 10–20 cm caps.
gymnopilus-spectabilis.holisticNotes: Contains psilocybin but often causes nausea; not a preferred species.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed contexts.
Extremely bitter — gastric distress common.
Confirm wood-growing habit vs. gilled lookalikes.

amanita-muscaria.habitat: Mycorrhizal with Douglas fir and pine — common in Eugene foothill forests and coastal woods near Florence.
amanita-muscaria.identification: Iconic red cap with white warts. White gills, ring on stem, bulbous base. Contains muscimol & ibotenic acid — NOT psilocybin.
amanita-muscaria.holisticNotes: One of the most recognizable mushrooms worldwide.
amanita-muscaria.preparation: Reference only — raw consumption is dangerous.
safetyWarnings: TOXIC if eaten raw — vomiting, confusion, hospitalization possible.
Amanita genus contains deadly species — expert ID essential.
Educational reference only.

amanita-pantherina.habitat: Conifer and hardwood forests in the PNW — valley to coast.
amanita-pantherina.identification: Brown cap with white warts. White gills and ring. Bulbous stem base in volva cup. Resembles fly agaric but cap is brown.
amanita-pantherina.holisticNotes: More potent muscimol content than A. muscaria.
safetyWarnings: HIGH RISK of severe poisoning — delirium, hospitalization.
Never consume. Document for ID education only.

panaeolus-cinctulus.habitat: Compost, manure-enriched soil, mulched gardens, and lawns — occasional in Eugene valley gardens.
panaeolus-cinctulus.identification: Small brown cap with darker band at margin when moist. Black gills mottled with spores. Grows from soil not wood.
panaeolus-cinctulus.holisticNotes: Weak to moderate psilocybin content — documented in Oregon.
panaeolus-cinctulus.harvestSeason: Spring through fall in enriched soils.
safetyWarnings: ILLEGAL outside licensed contexts.
Toxic lookalikes in Panaeolus genus — expert ID required.

datura-stramonium.habitat: Disturbed soil, vacant lots, roadsides, and gardens — occasional naturalized plant in the Willamette Valley.
datura-stramonium.identification: Large trumpet-shaped white or purple flowers. Spiky seed pods. Strong unpleasant odor. Large irregular toothed leaves.
datura-stramonium.holisticNotes: Deliriant tropane alkaloids — NOT a classic psychedelic. Historically associated with poisonings.
safetyWarnings: EXTREMELY DANGEROUS — overdose causes hospitalization, psychosis, death.
Educational reference only — avoid all ingestion.

blackcap-raspberry.habitat: Dry open slopes, forest edges, and disturbed ground from eastern Oregon through Klamath-Siskiyou and Sierra foothills.
blackcap-raspberry.identification: Arching canes with whitish bloom (glaucous) when young, turning dark purple-black. Compound leaves with 3–5 leaflets. Berries hollow when picked like black raspberry — not solid like blackberry.
lookalikes: Evergreen blackberry — solid aggregate fruit, persistent green leaves through winter.
Trailing blackberry — already in main library; smaller trailing canes.
Baneberry — white or red toxic berries on thick stalk; no cane structure.
blackcap-raspberry.edibleNotes: Intense sweet-tart flavor — excellent fresh, jam, or vinegar. Hollow core distinguishes from blackberries.
blackcap-raspberry.preparation: Eat fresh, freeze, or cook into jam. Wear gloves — canes have fine prickles.
safetyWarnings: Verify hollow berry core vs. solid blackberry aggregate.
Avoid berries near roads or sprayed areas.

evergreen-blackberry.habitat: Disturbed roadsides, fencerows, and open woods — widespread invasive in Willamette Valley and north-coast California.
evergreen-blackberry.identification: Deeply incised (laciniate) leaflets on vigorous thorny canes. White to pink flowers. Large aggregate black berries that stay solid when picked.
lookalikes: Himalayan blackberry (R. armeniacus) — larger rounded leaflets, not deeply cut.
Trailing blackberry — native, smaller, trailing habit.
Blackcap raspberry — hollow berry, whitish young canes.
evergreen-blackberry.edibleNotes: Abundant late-summer fruit — tart when underripe, sweet when fully black and soft.
evergreen-blackberry.preparation: Jam, pie, or freeze. Cook to soften seeds if desired.
safetyWarnings: Invasive species — harvest freely but do not spread canes.
Thorns are fierce — use thick gloves.

red-flowering-currant-berry.habitat: Open woods, bluffs, and forest edges — signature early-spring shrub of the coast and western valleys.
red-flowering-currant-berry.identification: Drooping clusters of pink to red tubular flowers in early spring. Maple-like lobed leaves with sticky glands. Dark blue-black berries with whitish bloom in summer.
lookalikes: Stink currant (R. bracteosum) — larger sticky flowers, skunky odor on bruised leaves.
Sierra gooseberry — spiny stems and prickly berries.
Any Ribes — learn leaf shape and flower timing.
red-flowering-currant-berry.edibleNotes: Berries are tart and seedy — best cooked into jelly or mixed with sweeter fruit. Flowers edible as garnish.
red-flowering-currant-berry.medicinalNotes: Traditional coastal peoples used bark and berries as tonics — consult experienced sources.
red-flowering-currant-berry.preparation: Cook berries with sugar for jelly. Flowers in salads (sparingly).
safetyWarnings: Raw berries are very tart — some people find them laxative in quantity.
Do not confuse with unrelated toxic shrubs.

stink-currant.habitat: Moist shady forest — coast range and Cascades understory.
stink-currant.identification: Large sticky-glandular greenish-white flower clusters. Strong skunky odor when leaves bruised. Dark purple-black berries.
lookalikes: Red-flowering currant — pink/red flowers, no skunk smell.
Sierra gooseberry — spiny stems.
Blue elderberry — flat flower cluster, not currant-like leaves.
stink-currant.edibleNotes: Berries edible cooked despite the name — flavor improves with heat and sugar. Not a fresh-eating berry.
stink-currant.preparation: Jelly or sauce only — always cook.
safetyWarnings: Skunky smell is normal — not a sign of spoilage.
Cook before eating — raw flavor is harsh.

sierra-gooseberry.habitat: Dry open pine and oak woodland — Klamath-Siskiyou and Sierra foothills.
sierra-gooseberry.identification: Spiny stems. Small lobed leaves. Purple-black berries covered in sharp spines — handle with care. Small greenish flowers.
lookalikes: Other gooseberries (Ribes) — all have spiny fruit; verify regional species.
Barberry — different leaf and spine pattern on branches.
sierra-gooseberry.edibleNotes: Tart spiny berries — classic gooseberry flavor once spines are removed by cooking and straining.
sierra-gooseberry.preparation: Cook and strain for jelly or pie filling. Never eat raw spiny fruit whole.
safetyWarnings: Spines on fruit can lodge in throat — always cook and strain.
Spiny stems — wear gloves.

chokecherry.habitat: Stream banks, canyon edges, and open slopes in eastern Oregon and Modoc/Sierra country.
chokecherry.identification: Oval serrated leaves. White fragrant flower racemes in spring. Dark purple-black cherries in hanging clusters. Bark often marked with lenticels.
lookalikes: Bitter cherry (P. emarginata) — larger, more bitter fruit; similar but different range.
Buckthorn — different leaf venation; berries not in cherry clusters.
Wild cherry pits contain cyanogenic compounds — never eat pits.
chokecherry.edibleNotes: Extremely astringent raw — name says it all. Excellent jelly, syrup, and pemmican ingredient when cooked.
chokecherry.medicinalNotes: Traditional bark tea — use only with expert guidance; bark contains compounds requiring careful preparation.
chokecherry.preparation: Cook fruit thoroughly. Strain out pits — NEVER crush or eat seeds (cyanide risk).
safetyWarnings: PITS CONTAIN CYANIDE — never eat, crush, or blend pits.
Raw fruit causes nausea — always cook.
Wilted leaves toxic to livestock — not for forage.

bitter-cherry.habitat: Forest edges and moist slopes from coast range through Cascades and into northern California.
bitter-cherry.identification: Small tree or large shrub. Oval leaves with rounded tips. White spring flowers. Bright red to dark red cherries — very bitter raw.
lookalikes: Chokecherry — darker purple fruit, more eastern distribution.
Oregon cherry relatives — all Prunus pits are toxic.
Holly — not a cherry; red berries on waxy leaves.
bitter-cherry.edibleNotes: Historically used cooked or dried by Indigenous peoples — extremely bitter raw. Mostly a survival or traditional food.
bitter-cherry.preparation: Cook thoroughly and strain. Discard all pits.
safetyWarnings: Pits contain cyanogenic glycosides — never eat or crush seeds.
Raw fruit is intensely bitter and may cause stomach upset.

madrone-berry.habitat: Dry open conifer and oak woodland — iconic peeling orange-red bark on coast and southwest Oregon.
madrone-berry.identification: Leathery evergreen leaves. Smooth peeling cinnamon bark. Clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers. Orange-red warty berries in fall.
lookalikes: Manzanita — similar flowers and berries but shrub form with smooth red bark, not peeling.
Toyon — serrated leaves, different bark.
madrone-berry.edibleNotes: Berries are mealy and bland-sweet — traditionally dried or made into cider-like drinks. High tannin when unripe.
madrone-berry.medicinalNotes: Traditional uses for leaves and berries — consult cultural and herbal sources.
madrone-berry.preparation: Wait until fully ripe (soft and red). Dry, ferment, or cook into jelly.
safetyWarnings: Unripe berries are astringent and high in tannins.
Eat in moderation — can be laxative.

manzanita-berry.habitat: Dry open pine and oak forest — eastern Cascades, Klamath, and Sierra foothills.
manzanita-berry.identification: Smooth red or brown bark on twisted stems. Leathery oval leaves. Pink-white urn flowers. Small red-brown apple-like berries.
lookalikes: Madrone — tree with peeling bark, larger berries.
Bearberry — ground-hugging, smaller range.
Toyon — tree/shrub with serrated leaves.
manzanita-berry.edibleNotes: Dry mealy "little apples" — traditionally ground into meal for mush or cider. Pleasant dry sweetness when ripe.
manzanita-berry.medicinalNotes: Leaves traditionally used as urinary antiseptic tea — strong tannin.
manzanita-berry.preparation: Dry berries and grind into flour, or soak for cider. Remove stones if grinding.
manzanita-berry.harvestSeason: Late summer–fall when deep red-brown and dry.
safetyWarnings: High tannin in unripe berries — wait until fully ripe.
Seeds are hard — grind or strain.

toyon.habitat: Chaparral, oak woodland, and coastal scrub in northern California — Sacramento Valley foothills to north coast.
toyon.identification: Evergreen shrub to small tree. Serrated holly-like leaf edges (not spiny). Clusters of small white flowers. Bright red berries in winter.
lookalikes: Holly — invasive; spiny leaves.
Manzanita — urn flowers, different leaf.
Pyracantha — thorny, non-native.
toyon.edibleNotes: Berries edible cooked — traditional cider and jelly. Raw berries cause GI upset for some.
toyon.medicinalNotes: Historical Native California uses — leaves and bark are astringent.
toyon.preparation: Cook berries for jelly or roast. Strain seeds.
safetyWarnings: Do not eat large quantities raw — can cause nausea.
Protected on some lands — check local rules.

wild-grape.habitat: Stream banks, riparian corridors, and forest edges — Rogue Valley and throughout northern California.
wild-grape.identification: Climbing vine with tendrils. Large lobed grape leaves. Small purple-black grapes in loose clusters. Shredding bark on older vines.
lookalikes: Virginia creeper — 5 leaflets, blue berries; oxalate crystals — toxic.
Poison ivy — "leaves of three" — no grape clusters.
Moonseed — single crescent seed — TOXIC.
wild-grape.edibleNotes: Small tart grapes — excellent wild wine, juice, and jelly. Seeds and skin add tannin.
wild-grape.preparation: Crush for juice/wine, or cook into jelly. Strain seeds.
safetyWarnings: CRITICAL: Check seeds — moonseed has a single crescent seed and is toxic.
Verify tendrils and grape leaf shape.

woodland-strawberry.habitat: Partial shade in forests, meadows, and trail edges — distinct from coastal beach strawberry.
woodland-strawberry.identification: Trifoliate toothed leaflets on thin runners. White five-petaled flowers. Small elongated red berries with seeds on surface — intense flavor.
lookalikes: Beach strawberry (F. chiloensis) — coastal dunes; in main library.
Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) — yellow flowers, bland hollow berry.
Cinquefoil — five leaflets, no sweet berry.
woodland-strawberry.edibleNotes: Tiny but explosively flavorful — among the best wild strawberries in the world.
woodland-strawberry.preparation: Eat fresh, or add to salads and desserts.
safetyWarnings: Yellow-flowered mock strawberry is not sweet — verify white flowers.

cascade-huckleberry.habitat: Subalpine meadows and open conifer forest — high Cascades and Mt. Shasta country.
cascade-huckleberry.identification: Deciduous shrub with bright green oval leaves turning red in fall. Pink-tinged bell flowers. Dark blue-purple berries with bloom.
lookalikes: Evergreen huckleberry (in main library) — evergreen leaves, lower elevation.
Dwarf huckleberry — smaller, often lower growing.
Red huckleberry (in main library) — grows on stumps, red stems.
cascade-huckleberry.edibleNotes: Choice subalpine berry — sweet-tart, excellent fresh or in pancakes.
cascade-huckleberry.preparation: Eat fresh, dry, or freeze. No cooking needed.
cascade-huckleberry.harvestSeason: Mid to late summer at elevation — August–September.
safetyWarnings: Harvest at legal elevations and permits on public land.
Bear country — make noise while picking.

dwarf-huckleberry.habitat: Alpine and subalpine meadows, rocky slopes — low mat-forming shrub.
dwarf-huckleberry.identification: Low mat-forming shrub only a few inches to a foot tall. Small oval leaves. Tiny blue-black berries with intense flavor.
lookalikes: Cascade huckleberry — taller shrub, larger berries.
Blueberries — cultivated or wild; similar but different growth habit.
dwarf-huckleberry.edibleNotes: Tiny powerhouse berries — labor-intensive to pick but exceptional flavor.
dwarf-huckleberry.preparation: Eat fresh or add to granola. Freeze for winter.
safetyWarnings: Alpine environment — weather changes fast.
Pick sustainably in fragile meadows.

osoberry.habitat: Earliest-blooming native shrub — moist forest edges and riparian zones valley to coast.
osoberry.identification: First white flower clusters in late winter. Slender leaves. Pea-sized peach-colored berries turning dark blue-black. Bitter almond scent when twigs scratched.
lookalikes: Cherry relatives — osoberry has dangling clusters and almond scent on twig.
Non-fruiting lookalikes in winter — learn twig and leaf shape.
osoberry.edibleNotes: Berries are mostly pit with thin flesh — bland to bitter. Historically eaten but not a choice fruit. First fresh berry of the season.
osoberry.medicinalNotes: Bark and bark tea used traditionally — expert knowledge required.
osoberry.preparation: Eat sparingly fresh when fully dark. Most foragers prefer later-season berries.
safetyWarnings: Pits should not be crushed — cyanogenic compounds like other Prunus relatives.
Flavor disappoints many — manage expectations.

western-dock.habitat: Moist meadows, stream banks, and spring wetlands — valley and eastern Oregon.
western-dock.identification: Basal rosette of large lance-shaped leaves. Tall seed stalks with rust-brown triangular seeds (tumbling). Sour taste from oxalic acid.
lookalikes: Curly dock (R. crispus) — wavy leaf margins; also edible.
Sheep sorrel (in main library) — smaller arrow-shaped leaves.
Lily-of-the-valley — TOXIC; not sour when chewed.
western-dock.edibleNotes: Young leaves add lemony tang to salads and soups. Seeds can be ground as flour substitute.
western-dock.preparation: Use young spring leaves. Cook to reduce oxalates for large servings.
western-dock.harvestSeason: Early spring leaves — March–April. Seeds: summer.
safetyWarnings: High oxalic acid — avoid large raw quantities if prone to kidney stones.
Do not confuse with non-sour toxic plants.

common-mallow.habitat: Disturbed soil, gardens, and roadsides — cosmopolitan weed in valley and California lowlands.
common-mallow.identification: Roundish lobed leaves on long petioles. Pink to white striped flowers. Disc-shaped "cheese" seed pods.
lookalikes: Other mallows — all generally edible in the Malva group.
Ground ivy — different square-stem mint smell.
common-mallow.edibleNotes: Mild mucilaginous leaves and young seed pods ("cheeses") — good in soups and as thickener.
common-mallow.medicinalNotes: Mucilage soothes throat and digestive tract — traditional demulcent.
common-mallow.preparation: Young leaves raw or cooked. Seed pods when still green and soft.
common-mallow.harvestSeason: Spring through fall — tender growth in spring best.
safetyWarnings: Forage away from contaminated urban soils.

sow-thistle.habitat: Disturbed ground, gardens, and field edges everywhere.
sow-thistle.identification: Milky sap when stem broken. Dandelion-like yellow flowers. Prickly-edged clasping stem leaves. Not a true thistle (no spines on stem).
lookalikes: Prickly lettuce — more spiny; also has milky sap.
True thistles — spiny all over; many edible after peeling.
Wild lettuce (in main library) — sedative sap; different uses.
sow-thistle.edibleNotes: Young leaves mild and good cooked like spinach — traditional Mediterranean pot herb.
sow-thistle.preparation: Boil or sauté young leaves. Change water if bitterness bothers you.
safetyWarnings: Milky sap — normal; not the same as wild lettuce sedative species.

prickly-lettuce.habitat: Dry disturbed roadsides, fields, and waste ground.
prickly-lettuce.identification: Tall upright plant with spiny midrib on underside of leaves. Milky white latex. Yellow dandelion-like flowers. Leaves often twist to orient vertically.
lookalikes: Wild lettuce (L. virosa / L. canadensis in main library) — stronger sedative latex.
Sow thistle — less prickly midrib.
True lettuce relatives — all have milky sap.
prickly-lettuce.edibleNotes: Young leaves before flowering — bitter but edible as cooked green. Older plants very bitter.
prickly-lettuce.preparation: Cook young leaves; blanch to reduce bitterness.
prickly-lettuce.harvestSeason: Early spring rosettes — before tall flowering stalk.
safetyWarnings: Bitter latex increases as plant ages — avoid large amounts of mature plant.
Not the same as recreational wild lettuce species.

watercress.habitat: Clean cold spring-fed streams and slow-moving water — must verify water quality.
watercress.identification: Low growing in water. Pinnately compound leaves with oval leaflets. White four-petaled flowers. Peppery taste when chewed.
lookalikes: Poison hemlock — TOXIC; musty smell, purple blotched stem, NOT peppery.
Water hemlock (Cicuta) — DEADLY; grows in same habitat.
Penny-cress and other cresses — peppery but different leaf shape.
watercress.edibleNotes: Classic peppery salad green — rich in vitamins and minerals.
watercress.medicinalNotes: Traditional spring tonic and digestive stimulant.
watercress.preparation: Raw in salads or briefly wilted in soup. Wash thoroughly.
watercress.harvestSeason: Year-round in mild springs — best spring growth.
safetyWarnings: NEVER harvest from polluted water — risk of liver fluke and bacteria.
Positive ID essential — hemlock grows in similar wet places and is DEADLY.
If in doubt, do not eat.

spring-beauty.habitat: Moist open forest and meadows — spring ephemerals in mountains and foothills.
spring-beauty.identification: Pair of narrow lance-shaped leaves. Delicate pink-striped white flowers. Small round corm (Indian potato) underground.
lookalikes: Other Claytonia species — generally edible.
False hellebore — TOXIC; much larger, different flower — know before digging.
spring-beauty.edibleNotes: Corms nutty and sweet raw or cooked — traditional Indigenous root food. Leaves also edible.
spring-beauty.preparation: Dig corms sustainably (small portion of patch). Roast or boil like mini potatoes.
safetyWarnings: Dig only where legal and sustainable — corms are slow to recover.
Verify not false hellebore before any root harvest.

nodding-onion.habitat: Dry open slopes and rocky outcrops — eastern Oregon and northern California.
nodding-onion.identification: Grass-like onion smell when crushed. Nodding pink flower umbels. Bulbs small and clustered.
lookalikes: Death camas (Zigadenus) — NO onion smell — TOXIC; grows in same areas as camas.
Other Allium — if it smells like onion/garlic, generally edible.
Grass — no onion odor when crushed.
nodding-onion.edibleNotes: Bulbs and leaves add mild onion flavor — smaller than cultivated onion.
nodding-onion.medicinalNotes: Same antimicrobial sulfur compounds as garlic/onion family.
nodding-onion.preparation: Use bulbs and leaves raw or cooked. Dried bulbs store well.
nodding-onion.harvestSeason: Spring–summer — after flowering for bulb size.
safetyWarnings: MUST smell onion/garlic — if no smell, do not eat (death camas rule).
Harvest sustainably — small bulbs.

wild-onion.habitat: Dry open grassland and sagebrush — east-side Oregon and Modoc/Sierra.
wild-onion.identification: Strong onion odor. Pink to purple flower umbel on short stem. Bulb with fibrous coat.
lookalikes: Death camas — NO onion smell — potentially FATAL.
Nodding onion — similar; both edible if onion-scented.
wild-onion.edibleNotes: Pungent wild onion bulbs — flavor punch in small packages.
wild-onion.preparation: Roast, pickle, or use fresh. Leaves also edible.
wild-onion.harvestSeason: Spring bulbs before flowering, or after seed set.
safetyWarnings: Onion smell test is mandatory every time.
Never harvest bulbs without confirming Allium identity.

fat-hen.habitat: Disturbed soil, gardens, and agricultural edges worldwide.
fat-hen.identification: Mealy white powder on young growing tips. Diamond-shaped toothed leaves with goosefoot shape. No red sap (unlike amaranth).
lookalikes: Lamb's quarters (in main library) — closely related; similar uses.
Orache — often reddish or arrow-shaped.
Nightshades — do not have mealy white coating.
fat-hen.edibleNotes: Top wild spinach — nutritious and mild when cooked.
fat-hen.preparation: Cook like spinach. Use only young tender tops.
safetyWarnings: Accumulates nitrates in polluted soil — avoid roadside patches.
Cook for best digestion.

wild-amaranth.habitat: Disturbed ground, gardens, and agricultural fields.
wild-amaranth.identification: Red taproot. Rough hairy stems. Large simple oval leaves. Tall green flower spikes maturing to black seeds.
lookalikes: Fat hen — mealy white tips, no red root.
Spiny amaranth — has spines at leaf nodes.
Prostrate pigweed — low spreading habit.
wild-amaranth.edibleNotes: Young leaves cooked like spinach. Seeds edible as grain (tiny but nutritious).
wild-amaranth.preparation: Cook leaves. Winnow seeds for grain or pop like miniature popcorn.
safetyWarnings: Avoid oxalate-heavy older leaves in huge quantities.
Spiny species require more prep.

orache.habitat: Disturbed alkaline soils and dry open ground — east-side and Great Basin fringe.
orache.identification: Arrowhead to diamond-shaped leaves, often gray-green or reddish. Mealy texture on some species. Insignificant green flowers.
lookalikes: Lamb's quarters / fat hen — similar goosefoot family.
Spinach — cultivated lookalike.
orache.edibleNotes: Mild salty spinach substitute — leaves can be red, green, or purple.
orache.preparation: Cook briefly or use young leaves raw in salad.
safetyWarnings: Salt-tolerant — may accumulate minerals; moderate portions.

winter-cress.habitat: Disturbed moist ground, ditches, and field margins.
winter-cress.identification: Basal rosette of lobed dark green leaves. Tall spikes of bright yellow four-petaled mustard flowers. Peppery mustard family taste.
lookalikes: Other Barbarea and bittercress — mustard family; generally similar prep.
Wild radish — similar flowers; hairier pods.
winter-cress.edibleNotes: Early spring green before bitterness intensifies — traditional "poor man's asparagus" for young shoots.
winter-cress.preparation: Boil young leaves and shoots; change water if too bitter.
winter-cress.harvestSeason: Early spring rosettes and flower shoots — March–April.
safetyWarnings: Becomes very bitter after flowering — harvest young.
Mustard family — goitrogens if eaten raw in huge amounts.

bittercress.habitat: Moist shady forest and stream edges — early spring groundcover.
bittercress.identification: Small pinnate leaves. Tiny white four-petaled flowers. Slender exploding seed pods when mature. Mild peppery taste.
lookalikes: Other Cardamine species — generally edible mustard family.
Winter cress — larger plant, yellow flowers.
bittercress.edibleNotes: Delicate peppery microgreen — excellent in spring salads.
safetyWarnings: Tiny plant — harvest sustainably in patches.

wild-radish-greens.habitat: Disturbed coastal and valley ground — fields, roadsides, and dunes.
wild-radish-greens.identification: Hairy leaves with lobed margins. Yellow or white four-petaled flowers (sometimes veined lavender). Jointed seed pods that do not split.
lookalikes: Wild mustard — smooth pods that split.
Rape/canola — similar yellow flowers.
wild-radish-greens.edibleNotes: Young leaves and flowers peppery like radish — good cooked green and salad garnish.
wild-radish-greens.preparation: Cook older leaves; young leaves raw. Pickled seed pods ("poor man's capers").
wild-radish-greens.harvestSeason: Spring greens and flowers; summer pods.
safetyWarnings: Hairy mature leaves are tough — use tender spring growth.

camas.habitat: Wet meadows and prairies — historically managed by Indigenous fire ecology in Willamette Valley.
camas.identification: Grass-like leaves from bulb. Tall spike of blue-violet six-petaled star flowers in spring. Bulb white and onion-shaped but NO onion smell.
lookalikes: DEATH CAMAS (Toxicoscordion venenosum / Zigadenus) — WHITE or cream flowers, NO onion smell — FATAL.
If flowers are white/cream and plant has NO onion odor — DO NOT HARVEST.
Onion family (Allium) — HAS onion smell — edible but different food.
camas.edibleNotes: Slow-roasted camas bulbs become sweet as pear — cornerstone Indigenous food of the Willamette Valley.
camas.medicinalNotes: Traditional food medicine — prepared only through long slow cooking.
camas.preparation: Pit-roast or slow bake 24–48 hours until brown and sweet. NEVER eat raw.
camas.harvestSeason: Dig bulbs after seed set — late summer when flowers are gone.
safetyWarnings: DEATH CAMAS grows in the same meadows — FATAL misidentification risk.
Camas has BLUE flowers; death camas has WHITE/CREAM flowers.
No onion smell on either — flower color and expert ID required.
Raw camas causes severe GI distress — always fully cook.
Never harvest without experienced mentor on first outings.

wapato.habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, ponds, and slow sloughs — wade to harvest.
wapato.identification: Arrowhead-shaped emergent leaves. Three-petaled white flowers. Round starchy tubers on underwater roots — pull or feel with toes.
lookalikes: Other Sagittaria — generally edible tubers.
Water hemlock roots in same habitat — DEADLY; know leaf shape.
Bur reed — different leaf and tuber.
wapato.edibleNotes: Starchy tubers like potatoes — historically traded extensively in the PNW.
wapato.preparation: Peel and boil or roast. Dried and ground as flour.
wapato.harvestSeason: Fall tuber harvest when tops die back.
safetyWarnings: Wade carefully — soft mud and deep holes.
Verify arrowhead leaf shape — not hemlock.

balsamroot.habitat: Dry open east-side hills and sagebrush — golden sunflower displays in spring.
balsamroot.identification: Large arrow-shaped fuzzy basal leaves. Big yellow sunflower-like blooms on short stems. Deep taproot and large fleshy root crown.
lookalikes: Mule's ears (Wyethia) — similar flowers; roots also historically used.
Sunflowers — different leaf and root.
balsamroot.edibleNotes: Roasted roots and seeds — piney-resinous flavor. Young leaf stems peeled and eaten.
balsamroot.medicinalNotes: Resinous root used in traditional salves and teas.
balsamroot.preparation: Slow-roast roots. Harvest seeds in summer. Peel young stems.
balsamroot.harvestSeason: Spring stems; fall roots; summer seeds.
safetyWarnings: Root harvest kills plant — take sparingly from large stands.
Resinous flavor is strong — start with small portions.

biscuitroot.habitat: Dry open woodland and rocky slopes — Klamath-Siskiyou and coast range.
biscuitroot.identification: Finely divided fern-like leaves. Yellow umbel flowers. Thick aromatic root smelling of celery/parsley when cut.
lookalikes: Poison hemlock and water hemlock — umbel family — DEADLY; no aromatic biscuitroot smell.
Other Lomatium — many edible with similar prep; expert ID helps.
Cow parsnip — much larger, different leaf.
biscuitroot.edibleNotes: Root dried and ground into flour for bread — traditional "biscuitroot" of the West.
biscuitroot.medicinalNotes: Lomatium species widely used in PNW herbalism — potent; consult qualified sources.
biscuitroot.preparation: Dry and grind root. Cook flour into cakes or thicken soups.
biscuitroot.harvestSeason: Fall root harvest after seeds set.
safetyWarnings: Umbel family — absolute certainty required vs. hemlock.
Some people report skin rash from handling — gloves recommended.

cow-parsnip.habitat: Moist meadows, stream banks, and forest openings — large leafy presence.
cow-parsnip.identification: Huge maple-like compound leaves. Thick hollow stem with purple mottling. Flat white umbel flowers — can reach 6+ feet tall.
lookalikes: GIANT HOGWEED (Heracleum mantegazzianum) — invasive; causes severe photodermatitis — AVOID.
Poison hemlock — purple blotched stem but fern-like leaves, not maple-like.
Cow parsnip leaf is MAPLE-SHAPED and huge.
cow-parsnip.edibleNotes: Young peeled leaf stalks and flower buds — celery-like when cooked. Traditional spring food.
cow-parsnip.preparation: COOK ONLY — peel young stems, boil or steam. Never eat raw.
cow-parsnip.harvestSeason: Early spring young stems — before flowers open.
safetyWarnings: NEVER EAT RAW — causes nausea.
Sap causes PHOTODERMATITIS (phytophotodermatitis) — wear gloves; avoid sun on skin contact.
Do not confuse with giant hogweed.
Only young spring growth — older plant becomes inedible and more toxic.

silverweed.habitat: Coastal estuaries, tidal flats, and moist meadows — silver-backed pinnate leaves.
silverweed.identification: Pinnate leaves with silvery white undersides. Yellow five-petaled buttercup-family flowers. Creeping red runners. Small edible roots.
lookalikes: Cinquefoil — similar flowers but no silver leaf backs.
Strawberry — trifoliate, not pinnate.
silverweed.edibleNotes: Roots sweet and starchy when slow-cooked — traditional coastal food. Leaves edible in moderation.
silverweed.preparation: Slow-roast or steam roots until soft and sweet.
silverweed.harvestSeason: Fall and winter roots when tops dormant.
safetyWarnings: Sustainable harvest — roots are small; take sparingly.
Buttercup family — always cook roots.

lady-fern-fiddleheads.habitat: Moist shady forest and stream banks — one of the most common ferns in the PNW.
lady-fern-fiddleheads.identification: Bright green lacy fronds. Fiddleheads emerge in spring as tightly coiled green crosiers with brown papery scales (not black like bracken).
lookalikes: Bracken fern — triangular fronds, black stem on fiddlehead; carcinogenic concerns.
Ostrich fern (E. esculentum) — edible; deep U-shaped groove on stem.
Unidentified fern fiddleheads — do not eat without species ID.
lady-fern-fiddleheads.edibleNotes: Mild fiddleheads — popular spring green when properly cooked.
lady-fern-fiddleheads.preparation: Remove brown scales. Boil 10+ minutes or steam, then sauté. Never raw.
safetyWarnings: Never eat raw — thiaminase and other compounds.
Confirm species — not all ferns are edible.

deer-fern.habitat: Moist conifer forest floor — two distinct frond types (fertile brownish upright, sterile flat green).
deer-fern.identification: Sterile fronds flat rosette near ground. Fertile fronds taller, narrow, with rolled-under pinnae bearing spores. Leathery texture.
lookalikes: Other woodland ferns — deer fern has unique dual frond types.
Sword fern — single frond type, larger.
deer-fern.edibleNotes: Rhizomes and young fronds historically eaten — minor food; more medicinal than staple.
deer-fern.medicinalNotes: Coastal peoples used rhizome chews for mouth sores and digestive support.
deer-fern.preparation: Cook rhizomes thoroughly if used. Young fronds cooked like greens.
safetyWarnings: Not a beginner fern food — cook thoroughly.
Harvest rhizomes sustainably — slow-growing.

bracken-fiddleheads.habitat: Disturbed sunny slopes, roadsides, and forest openings — aggressive colonizer.
bracken-fiddleheads.identification: Triangular fronds on tall stems. Fiddleheads with black/brown stem base and woolly coating. Single type of frond (not deer fern's dual form).
lookalikes: Lady fern — lacy, not triangular; green stem on fiddlehead.
Ostrich fern — U-groove on stem.
bracken-fiddleheads.edibleNotes: Eaten in many cultures when heavily processed — controversial due to carcinogen (ptaquiloside) research.
bracken-fiddleheads.preparation: Boil in multiple changes of water 15+ minutes. Traditional soaking and salt-curing in some cultures.
safetyWarnings: CONTAINS PTAQUILOSIDE — linked to cancer in animal studies; epidemiological concerns in heavy consumers.
Never eat raw. Extensive cooking required.
Many foragers avoid entirely — eat at your own informed risk.
Do not pickle without proper processing.

wild-hazelnut.habitat: Understory of moist forest — coast range and Cascades.
wild-hazelnut.identification: Double-toothed oval leaves. Long beaked husk enclosing small nut. Catkins in winter. Often multi-stemmed shrub.
lookalikes: Cultivated hazelnut — larger nuts, shorter husk.
Other Corylus — all edible nuts in genus.
wild-hazelnut.edibleNotes: Small but rich wild nuts — ripen before husks turn fully brown (jays compete for them).
wild-hazelnut.preparation: Dry and crack. Roast for best flavor. Ground into meal.
wild-hazelnut.harvestSeason: Late summer — August–September before jays take them all.
safetyWarnings: Harvest green-turning-brown before wildlife does.
Husk hairs can irritate skin.

garry-oak-acorn.habitat: Open oak savanna and woodland — Willamette Valley and Rogue oak country.
garry-oak-acorn.identification: Deeply lobed oak leaves. Acorns short-stalked with shallow scaly cap. Large spreading oak of valley floors.
lookalikes: Other oak acorns — all require leaching; species vary in tannin.
Horse chestnut/buckeye — NOT an oak; TOXIC without proper ID.
garry-oak-acorn.edibleNotes: Staple Indigenous carbohydrate — sweet after proper leaching compared to many oaks.
garry-oak-acorn.preparation: Shell, grind, and LEACH tannins in cold or hot water repeatedly until not bitter. Then bake into mush or flour.
safetyWarnings: RAW ACORNS ARE INEDIBLE — high tannins cause nausea and kidney stress.
Leaching is mandatory — cold water leaching (days) or hot (repeated boils).
Never skip leaching step.

golden-chinquapin.habitat: Dry open conifer forest — understory shrub to small tree on coast and Cascades.
golden-chinquapin.identification: Evergreen serrated leaves with golden fuzzy undersides. Spiny bur enclosing single sweet nut.
lookalikes: Chestnut burs — related; similar spiny husk.
Tanoak — different leaf; acorn not single nut in spiny bur.
golden-chinquapin.edibleNotes: Sweet nut edible raw or roasted — one of the best wild nuts in the PNW.
golden-chinquapin.preparation: Roast in oven or open fire. Remove from spiny bur with gloves.
safetyWarnings: Spiny burs — wear gloves.
Competes with squirrels — harvest promptly.

gray-pine-nut.habitat: Hot dry foothill woodland — Sacramento Valley edges and Sierra west slope.
gray-pine-nut.identification: Large heavy cones with hooked spines. Long gray-green needles in bundles of three. Irregular open crown.
lookalikes: Other pine nuts — all require work to extract.
Ponderosa pine — lighter cones, different range.
gray-pine-nut.edibleNotes: Large nutritious pine nuts — traditional California Indigenous staple.
gray-pine-nut.preparation: Roast cones to open, or hammer nuts from cones. Shell small nuts patiently.
safetyWarnings: Heavy spiny cones — watch your head under trees.
Labor-intensive shelling.
