chia.habitat: Dry open grassland and sagebrush — east-side Oregon fringe and California foothills.
chia.identification: Square mint-family stem. Small blue flowers in spiky whorls. Tiny seeds in calyx cups — swell in water.
lookalikes: Other Salvia — mint smell on crushed leaves.
Non-mint lookalikes — verify square stem and mint odor.
chia.edibleNotes: Seeds form gel when soaked — protein and omega-3 rich. Traditional pemmican and beverage ingredient.
chia.medicinalNotes: Cooling demulcent seed gel — traditional thirst quencher on hot trails.
chia.preparation: Winnow seeds. Soak in water for gel drink, or grind into meal.
chia.harvestSeason: Summer when seed heads dry — June–July.
safetyWarnings: Ensure fully dry seeds for storage — mold risk if damp.

spruce-tips.habitat: Coastal and montane conifer forest — harvest from Sitka spruce on coast, Engelmann/blue spruce east-side.
spruce-tips.identification: Soft bright green new growth at branch tips in spring. Single sharp needles. Hanging cones. Citrus-resin scent when crushed.
lookalikes: Fir tips — flat friendly needles (not sharp), different cone upright on branch.
Yew — flat dark needles, red cup berry — TOXIC.
Douglas fir (in main library) — bracts on cones, different needle.
spruce-tips.edibleNotes: Bright citrus-pine flavor — syrup, beer, salt, and tea. High vitamin C.
spruce-tips.medicinalNotes: Resinous tea for respiratory support — similar to fir tips.
spruce-tips.preparation: Infuse in syrup, honey, or vinegar. Dry for tea.
safetyWarnings: Take only tips from lower branches — never top trees.
Sharp needles — handle gently.

grand-fir-tips.habitat: Low to mid-elevation moist forest — west-side valleys and coast range.
grand-fir-tips.identification: Flat needles with two white stomatal bands underneath — no prickles (friendly fir). Upright cones on branches. Balsam-scented blister resin on bark.
lookalikes: Douglas fir — not a true fir; single bracts on cones.
Spruce — sharp square needles rolled in fingers.
Hemlock — small cones, different needle arrangement.
grand-fir-tips.edibleNotes: Grapefruit-balsam flavored tips — among the best conifer tips for syrup and tea.
grand-fir-tips.medicinalNotes: Balsam resin traditionally used topically; tip tea for chest congestion.
grand-fir-tips.preparation: Spring tip syrup, tea, or infused salt.
safetyWarnings: Sustainable harvest — few tips per branch.

bigleaf-maple-sap.habitat: Moist lowland forest — dominant maple of west-side riparian zones.
bigleaf-maple-sap.identification: Largest leaves of any maple — up to 12 inches across. Five lobes. Winged samaras in pairs. Moss-covered branches common.
lookalikes: Vine maple — smaller leaves, shrubbier.
Other maples — all produce sap but bigleaf is the PNW species.
bigleaf-maple-sap.edibleNotes: Sap makes delicate syrup — lower sugar than sugar maple but unique flavor. Also sap drink fresh.
bigleaf-maple-sap.preparation: Tap in late winter. Boil sap down 40:1 or more for syrup.
bigleaf-maple-sap.harvestSeason: Late winter sap run — February–March during freeze-thaw cycles.
safetyWarnings: Tap only healthy large trees — small hole, proper spile.
Boil sap outdoors — heavy steam.

yerba-buena.habitat: Shady forest floor trailing vine — coast range and lowland forest.
yerba-buena.identification: Trailing square-stemmed mint with tiny rounded leaves. Strong mint aroma when crushed. Small white flowers.
lookalikes: Wild mint (in main library) — upright, larger leaves.
Other mints — mint smell confirms family.
yerba-buena.edibleNotes: Classic PNW forest tea — mild mint flavor. Leaves for tea and garnish.
yerba-buena.medicinalNotes: Cooling digestive tea — traditional stomach soother.
yerba-buena.preparation: Fresh or dried leaf tea. Cold infusion preferred by some.
yerba-buena.harvestSeason: Spring through fall — year-round in mild coast.
safetyWarnings: Trailing habit — harvest from clean forest floor.

mugwort.habitat: Stream banks, open woodland, and disturbed moist ground.
mugwort.identification: Tall aromatic silvery-green leaves, white-woolly underneath. Pungent sage-camphor smell. Small greenish flower spikes.
lookalikes: Wormwood (A. absinthium) — more silvery, bitter.
Other Artemisia — aromatic family; verify regional species.
mugwort.edibleNotes: Used as bitter aromatic seasoning in small amounts — rice cakes and mochi wrapping in Asian traditions.
mugwort.medicinalNotes: Dream pillow herb, moxibustion, and digestive bitter — powerful; not for pregnancy.
mugwort.preparation: Small amounts as food seasoning. Dry for tea or dream sachets.
safetyWarnings: AVOID IN PREGNANCY — stimulates uterus.
Strong herb — small culinary doses only.

sweet-cicely.habitat: Moist shady forest — understory of conifer and mixed woods.
sweet-cicely.identification: Fern-like divided leaves with anise-licorice smell when crushed. Small white umbel flowers. Long slender aromatic roots.
lookalikes: Poison hemlock — NO anise smell — DEADLY.
Other Osmorhiza — anise scent confirms edible group.
Sweet cicely vs. hemlock: CRUSH AND SMELL — anise = sweet cicely.
sweet-cicely.edibleNotes: Anise-flavored roots, leaves, and green seeds — natural sweetener quality.
sweet-cicely.medicinalNotes: Soothing stomach herb — anise flavor aids digestion.
sweet-cicely.preparation: Use young leaves and seeds in salads. Cook roots or chew as trail nibble.
sweet-cicely.harvestSeason: Spring leaves; fall roots; early summer green seeds.
safetyWarnings: Anise smell is critical ID vs. hemlock.
Umbel family — never eat without smell test.

california-bay-laurel.habitat: Moist canyon woodland — southwest Oregon and northern California.
california-bay-laurel.identification: Evergreen lance leaves with peppery bay aroma when crushed. Yellow-green four-petaled flowers. Green oval drupes.
lookalikes: Mediterranean bay laurel — similar smell but cultivated; smaller leaves.
Madrona — different bark and berry.
california-bay-laurel.edibleNotes: Leaves used SPARINGLY as spice — much stronger than Mediterranean bay. Nuts roasted (after leaching).
california-bay-laurel.medicinalNotes: Headache remedy in some traditions — volatile oils are potent.
california-bay-laurel.preparation: Use 1/4 the amount of regular bay leaves. Roast nuts after leaching like acorns.
safetyWarnings: Leaves are VERY strong — overuse causes headache and nausea.
Use sparingly in cooking — start with tiny amounts.
Headache tree nickname is literal.

bull-kelp.habitat: Pacific sub-tidal and low intertidal — floating canopy with bulb and long stipe from rocky coast.
bull-kelp.identification: Large floating bulb at surface connected to long stipe. Broad blade fronds. Grows in kelp forests visible from shore.
lookalikes: Other kelp species — generally edible with similar prep.
Detritus or drift — harvest fresh attached or recently washed up cold.
bull-kelp.edibleNotes: Stipe pickles ("kelp pickles"), dried flakes for dashi, and fresh fronds in soups.
bull-kelp.preparation: Pickle stipes, dry fronds for seasoning, or blanch before use.
safetyWarnings: Check local harvest rules and limits.
Only from clean cold ocean water.
Slippery on rocks — safety first.

sea-palm.habitat: Surf-swept rocky headlands — only where waves crash. Iconic tufted kelp looks like tiny palm trees.
sea-palm.identification: Short stipe with dense cluster of finger-like fronds. Only on exposed surf zones. Distinctive palm-tree silhouette.
lookalikes: Other small kelps — sea palm is uniquely surf-zone and palm-shaped.
sea-palm.edibleNotes: Prized crunchy texture — eaten raw or dried. Commercially popular PNW seaweed snack.
sea-palm.preparation: Rinse and eat raw, roast until crisp, or add to soups.
sea-palm.harvestSeason: Summer low tides on calm days.
safetyWarnings: HARVEST ONLY WITH EXTREME CAUTION — surf zone is dangerous.
Protected in some areas — check regulations.
Never turn back to the ocean on slippery rocks.

sea-lettuce.habitat: Intertidal rocks, tide pools, and sheltered bays — bright green sheets.
sea-lettuce.identification: Bright green thin ruffled sheets resembling lettuce. No midrib. Soft texture when fresh.
lookalikes: Enteromorpha (Ulva) species — similar edible greens.
Green algae films — verify sheet structure.
sea-lettuce.edibleNotes: Mild green salad seaweed — raw in salads or dried as flakes.
sea-lettuce.preparation: Rinse well. Raw in salads or brief blanch. Dry for seasoning.
sea-lettuce.harvestSeason: Spring through fall — bright green growth.
safetyWarnings: Do not harvest from polluted bays — absorbs nutrients/toxins.
Rinse sand thoroughly.

bladderwrack.habitat: Mid intertidal rocky shore — branched fronds with paired float bladders.
bladderwrack.identification: Olive-brown branched fronds with midrib and paired air bladders that pop when squeezed. Forked tips.
lookalikes: Other Fucus species — similar and edible.
Sargassum — different range (more southern).
bladderwrack.edibleNotes: Blanched fronds as vegetable. Bladders pop for fun trail snack. Rich in minerals.
bladderwrack.medicinalNotes: Traditional iodine and thyroid support source — moderation essential.
bladderwrack.preparation: Blanch or pickle. Use in broth. Dry for powder.
safetyWarnings: Iodine content — avoid excess if thyroid sensitive.
Clean ocean only.

nori-laver.habitat: High intertidal rocks — thin purple-red film to ruffled sheets.
nori-laver.identification: Purple-red to greenish thin sheet algae on rocks. Nearly translucent when fresh. Same genus as sushi nori.
lookalikes: Other Porphyra/Pyropia — all generally edible laver types.
Irish moss — different texture.
nori-laver.edibleNotes: Classic nori when dried — toast on skillet until crisp. Traditional "black butter" and sheets.
nori-laver.preparation: Dry and toast into nori sheets, or fry fresh in butter.
nori-laver.harvestSeason: Winter and spring growth — best after storms.
safetyWarnings: Rinse grit thoroughly.
Harvest from clean surf-exposed rocks.

rockweed.habitat: High intertidal splash zone on rocks — small olive fronds with pointed tips, no bladders.
rockweed.identification: Small forked olive-brown fronds with distinctive pointed tips. No air bladders (unlike Fucus). Grows above barnacle zone.
lookalikes: Bladderwrack (Fucus) — has paired bladders.
Other high-zone seaweeds — verify forked tips.
rockweed.edibleNotes: Tender tips in spring — steamed or added to broth. Traditional coastal nibble.
rockweed.preparation: Steam tips or dry for broth powder.
safetyWarnings: Small harvests — intertidal zone stewardship.
Clean water only.

pickleweed.habitat: Salt marshes and tidal flats — jointed succulent stems in saline wetlands.
pickleweed.identification: Jointed succulent green-to-red stems resembling tiny cactus without spines. No true leaves visible. Grows in salt marsh.
lookalikes: Other Salicornia — all generally edible salt marsh plants.
Sea blite — different branching.
pickleweed.edibleNotes: Crisp salty "sea asparagus" — blanch or pickle. Trendy restaurant green from wild marshes.
pickleweed.preparation: Blanch 30 seconds, sauté in butter, or pickle in vinegar.
safetyWarnings: Salt marsh only — do not confuse with inland plants.
Check tidal access safety.

sea-rocket.habitat: Sandy beaches and dunes above high tide line.
sea-rocket.identification: Fleshy succulent leaves on sand. Four-petaled white to lavender flowers. Peppery mustard-family taste. Pod splits into two corky segments.
lookalikes: Beach mustard — similar habitat and family.
Orach on dunes — different leaf shape.
sea-rocket.edibleNotes: Peppery succulent leaves and young seed pods — beach salad green.
sea-rocket.preparation: Raw in salads or quick pickle of pods.
safetyWarnings: Dune habitat fragile — step carefully on established paths.
Rinse sand.

elderflower.habitat: Same as blue elderberry — stream banks, open woods, sunny edges. Flower harvest is separate focus from berry entry in main library.
elderflower.identification: Large flat cream-white flower clusters (corymbs) in late spring. Compound opposite leaves. Reddish stems. Must confirm blue elder, NOT red elder.
lookalikes: Red elderberry (S. racemosa) — upright CONICAL red-fruited cluster later; flowers similar — TOXIC berries.
Blue elder (S. cerulea) — flat flower cluster, blue berries later.
Red elder flowers in conical cluster; blue elder flowers in flat broad corymb.
elderflower.edibleNotes: Floral fritters, cordial, and champagne — classic spring delicacy. Remove most stems.
elderflower.medicinalNotes: Cooling diaphoretic flower tea — traditional fever support.
elderflower.preparation: Infuse flowers in syrup, cordial, or batter for fritters. Strain out insects and stems.
safetyWarnings: Confirm BLUE elder (S. cerulea) — flat flower cluster.
RED elder (S. racemosa) has conical flower/berry cluster — berries TOXIC raw.
Do not eat large amounts of stems or leaves — cyanogenic compounds.

nootka-rose-hips.habitat: Focus on fall hip harvest from stream banks and sunny openings — complements the main library Nootka rose entry with hip-specific foraging detail.
nootka-rose-hips.identification: Large red-orange rose hips with persistent sepals at tip. Thorny stems. Hips round to pear-shaped, 1–2 cm. Seeds and hairs inside.
lookalikes: Baldhip rose (R. gymnocarpa) — hips lose sepals early; same hair caution.
Himalayan blackberry fruit — aggregate, not a hip.
nootka-rose-hips.edibleNotes: Among the highest vitamin C wild foods — tart apple-like flavor in tea, syrup, and jelly.
nootka-rose-hips.medicinalNotes: Astringent hip tea for digestive and winter immune support.
nootka-rose-hips.preparation: Halve and scrape out hairy seeds, or cook whole and strain through jelly bag. Never eat hairs.
nootka-rose-hips.harvestSeason: After first frost — October–November when fully colored.
safetyWarnings: IRRITATING HAIRS inside hips — always strain or scoop out seeds and hairs.
Do not eat hips whole without processing.

white-chanterelle.habitat: Mature conifer forests — Douglas-fir and hemlock from Oregon Cascades through the Klamath-Siskiyou and north-coast California.
white-chanterelle.identification: Pale cream to buff funnel cap with false forked ridges (not true gills). Fruity apricot scent. Stems often stocky and off-center.
lookalikes: Golden chanterelle — more orange; same false gill rule.
Jack-o-lantern (Omphalotus) — true gills, grows on wood in clusters, bioluminescent — TOXIC.
False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis) — thin true gills, no apricot smell.
white-chanterelle.edibleNotes: Choice edible — firmer and nuttier than golden chanterelle. Dries and sautés beautifully.
white-chanterelle.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Brush clean; avoid waterlogging.
white-chanterelle.harvestSeason: Fall after first heavy rains — October–December.
safetyWarnings: Confirm false gills vs. true gills every time.
Never eat raw.

yellowfoot-chanterelle.habitat: Mossy conifer logs and wet needle litter — late-season coast and valley forests.
yellowfoot-chanterelle.identification: Small brownish funnel cap with yellow-orange hollow stem. False gills on cap underside. Often in large troops on rotting wood.
lookalikes: False chanterelle — brighter orange, not hollow stem.
Toxic small brown gilled mushrooms on wood — always verify hollow stem + false ridges.
yellowfoot-chanterelle.edibleNotes: Excellent in soups and stews — holds texture when simmered. Less fruity than golden chanterelle.
yellowfoot-chanterelle.preparation: Simmer in broth or sauté; pairs with cream and potatoes.
yellowfoot-chanterelle.harvestSeason: Late fall through winter — November–February on wet coast.
safetyWarnings: Small size makes ID harder — use magnifier on gill structure.

black-trumpet.habitat: Mossy hardwood and mixed forest floors — often near oak and madrone in northerly California foothills.
black-trumpet.identification: Thin blackish-gray vase- or trumpet-shaped cap with smooth underside (no gills). Fragile, papery flesh.
lookalikes: Very few lookalikes when trumpet shape confirmed — avoid any with true gills.
Urnula craterium (devil’s urn) — spring cup fungus on wood; inedible but different season/habitat.
black-trumpet.edibleNotes: Intense earthy flavor — prized dried. Excellent in sauces and risotto.
black-trumpet.preparation: Dry whole or sauté; rehydrate dried trumpets in warm water.
safetyWarnings: Hard to spot against leaf litter — go slow and use basket.

king-bolete.habitat: Under pine and fir — eastern Oregon Cascades, Klamath-Silver Lake country, Mt. Shasta, and Sierra pine belts near Placerville.
king-bolete.identification: Large brown bun cap, thick white stem with fine reticulation (net pattern). Pores under cap white then yellow-green — NOT red/blue staining badly.
lookalikes: Bitter bolete (Caloboletus) — intensely bitter; blue-staining pores.
Satan’s bolete (Rubroboletus) — red pores on mature cap — TOXIC.
False king bolete — learn pore color and reticulation with a mentor.
king-bolete.edibleNotes: Premier gourmet mushroom — nutty when young, best dried for year-round use.
king-bolete.preparation: Slice and dry, or grill thick slices. Remove wormy sections.
king-bolete.harvestSeason: Early fall — September–November after rain under pines.
safetyWarnings: Bolete rule: avoid red-pored or rapid blue-bruising species unless expert ID.
Cut every cap to check for maggots.

spring-king-bolete.habitat: Ponderosa pine and mixed conifer — spring snowmelt zones from Rogue Valley to Modoc and Sierra foothills.
spring-king-bolete.identification: Large brown cap, stout stem with reticulation. Spring fruiting. Pores yellow. Similar to king bolete but earlier season.
lookalikes: Bitter boletes — taste test tiny raw nibble at tip of cap (spit out) only if experienced.
Satan’s bolete — red pores.
spring-king-bolete.edibleNotes: Excellent spring porcini relative — firmer texture than fall king.
spring-king-bolete.preparation: Grill or dry. Check for larvae when cutting.
safetyWarnings: Spring boletes still require full pore and staining checks.

admirable-bolete.habitat: On rotting conifer logs and stumps — classic Pacific Northwest log bolete.
admirable-bolete.identification: Velvety brown cap. Yellow pores bruise blue. Grows directly from wood (not soil). Stem often curved.
lookalikes: Other blue-staining boletes on wood — some bitter; admirable is considered good when young.
Conifer chicken of the woods grows on same logs — bright orange shelves.
admirable-bolete.edibleNotes: Oregon coast specialty on old-growth logs — nutty when young and firm.
admirable-bolete.preparation: Sauté young specimens; discard soft or wormy flesh.
safetyWarnings: Only young firm caps — becomes buggy and soft quickly.

zellers-bolete.habitat: Mixed conifer-hardwood forest floor — common in Douglas-fir and hemlock woods.
zellers-bolete.identification: Dark brown cracked cap, yellow pores that bruise blue, red-stained base of stem. Medium-sized bolete.
lookalikes: Other small boletes — use field guides for pore color and cap cracking pattern.
zellers-bolete.edibleNotes: Solid table mushroom when young — earthy and mild.
zellers-bolete.preparation: Cook thoroughly; remove slimy cap cuticle if preferred.
safetyWarnings: Blue bruising is normal for this species — do not confuse with red-pored toxic boletes.

chicken-of-the-woods.habitat: On living or dead hardwoods and conifers — oak, eucalyptus, and fir stumps.
chicken-of-the-woods.identification: Bright orange-yellow overlapping shelf brackets. Soft suede-like surface when young. No gills — porous yellow underside.
lookalikes: Jack-o-lantern (Omphalotus) — grows on wood but has GILLS and bioluminescence — TOXIC.
Dryad’s saddle — scaly brown cap, different texture.
chicken-of-the-woods.edibleNotes: Meaty texture — shreds like chicken. Only eat young tender margins.
chicken-of-the-woods.preparation: Sauté, bread and fry, or simmer in curry. Avoid alcohol with some individuals (rare sensitivity).
chicken-of-the-woods.harvestSeason: Spring through fall on fresh growth — May–October.
safetyWarnings: Never eat growing on eucalyptus or locust without caution — some report reactions.
Only young soft orange edges — woody older parts cause GI upset.

lobster-mushroom.habitat: Parasite on russulas and lactarius — forest floor and trails in mixed woods.
lobster-mushroom.identification: Bright orange-red bumpy crust completely covering host mushroom. No visible gills — looks like sculpted seafood.
lookalikes: Any orange mushroom without confirmed parasite crust on a host — must be Hypomyces over white mushroom host.
Do not confuse with unrelated orange gilled species.
lobster-mushroom.edibleNotes: Dense seafood-like texture — excellent in chowder and pasta.
lobster-mushroom.preparation: Cook thoroughly; dice and sauté. Host identity obscured — only collect pristine specimens.
safetyWarnings: If parasite not complete or host unknown, skip.
Cook well.

hedgehog-mushroom.habitat: Mossy conifer and mixed woods — often near chanterelle habitat.
hedgehog-mushroom.identification: Pale orange-tan cap with TEETH (spines) underneath instead of gills or pores. Fruity smell when fresh.
lookalikes: Toothed hedgehog relatives — Hydnum umbilicatum smaller with central depression.
No deadly lookalikes with teeth under cap in PNW — still verify every collection.
hedgehog-mushroom.edibleNotes: Mild sweet flavor — excellent sautéed with butter.
hedgehog-mushroom.preparation: Brush clean; cook until golden. Holds shape well.
safetyWarnings: Teeth, not gills — key ID feature.

lions-mane.habitat: On hardwood logs and wounds — bigleaf maple, oak, and beech in northerly California.
lions-mane.identification: White cascading icicle-like teeth hanging from a single attachment point. No cap. Looks like a frozen waterfall.
lookalikes: Other Hericium species — all considered edible in PNW when fresh and white.
Do not confuse with polypore brackets — Hericium is tooth-bearing soft mass.
lions-mane.edibleNotes: Crab-like texture when sautéed — gourmet and medicinal (nerve support studies).
lions-mane.medicinalNotes: Traditional use for cognitive and nerve support — lion’s mane widely studied.
lions-mane.preparation: Slice steaks and pan-fry until edges crisp. Also dual-extract for tincture.
safetyWarnings: Only fresh white specimens — yellow/brown indicates decay.

bears-head-hericium.habitat: On conifer logs and stumps — fir and hemlock in coastal and montane forests.
bears-head-hericium.identification: Branching white coral-like teeth — more branched than lion’s mane. Grows on conifers.
lookalikes: Other Hericium — generally edible group in our region.
bears-head-hericium.edibleNotes: Similar to lion’s mane — excellent texture. PNW conifer specialist.
bears-head-hericium.preparation: Sauté or simmer in soup. Harvest young white clusters.
bears-head-hericium.harvestSeason: Late summer through fall on logs.
safetyWarnings: Confirm growth on wood and tooth structure.

oyster-mushroom.habitat: On dead hardwood and cottonwood — logs, stumps, and standing snags.
oyster-mushroom.identification: Shelf-like caps growing in overlapping clusters. White gills running down short stem. Lilac-gray spore print.
lookalikes: Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) on conifer — historically eaten but linked to fatalities in Japan — AVOID on hemlock.
Omphalotus — bright orange, grows on wood, bioluminescent — TOXIC.
oyster-mushroom.edibleNotes: Mild anise-like flavor — farmed and wild. Great stir-fried.
oyster-mushroom.preparation: Cook on high heat until edges crisp. Discard tough stems if desired.
oyster-mushroom.harvestSeason: Year-round on logs; peak fall and spring flushes.
safetyWarnings: NEVER collect white gilled mushrooms on conifer as “oysters” — angel wings risk.
Stick to hardwood-hosted clusters with lilac spore print.

western-giant-puffball.habitat: Open sagebrush-steppe and dry grassland — eastern Oregon, Modoc, and Great Basin fringes of northerly California.
western-giant-puffball.identification: Huge white ball on ground — soccer-ball size possible. Interior solid white when young. No stem or gills.
lookalikes: Death cap button stage (Amanita) — MUST slice vertically — amanita has forming cap inside.
Earthball (Scleroderma) — dark interior when young — TOXIC.
western-giant-puffball.edibleNotes: Only edible when interior pure white like marshmallow. Earthy slices fried like eggplant.
western-giant-puffball.preparation: Peel skin; slice and fry breaded cutlets. Never eat if interior yellowing.
western-giant-puffball.harvestSeason: Late summer after thunderstorms — August–September in high desert.
safetyWarnings: ALWAYS cut in half — if any silhouette of cap/stem inside, discard (Amanita button).
Yellow-green interior = too mature — do not eat.

gem-studded-puffball.habitat: Wood chip trails, forest edges, and disturbed soil — very common.
gem-studded-puffball.identification: Small white pear-shaped puffball with conical spines that rub off. Interior white when young. Grows on ground.
lookalikes: Young earthballs — interior turns dark early; cut every puffball in half.
Amanita egg stage — shows cap forming inside when sliced.
gem-studded-puffball.edibleNotes: Snack-sized — sauté whole young specimens or add to breakfast scrambles.
gem-studded-puffball.preparation: Only pure white interior. Peel optional.
safetyWarnings: Slice vertically before eating any puffball.

shaggy-mane.habitat: Disturbed ground — gravel roads, lawns, compost, and trail edges after rain.
shaggy-mane.identification: Tall cylindrical white cap with shaggy scales. Deliquesces to black ink when old. Free white gills. Bulbous base.
lookalikes: Other inky caps — some with alcohol interaction; shaggy mane is the safest well-known species.
Green-spored parasol (Chlorophyllum) — much larger, green spores — TOXIC.
shaggy-mane.edibleNotes: Delicate flavor — must cook same day while caps still white.
shaggy-mane.preparation: Sauté quickly after harvest. Do not combine with alcohol (related species issue — caution).
shaggy-mane.harvestSeason: Spring and fall flushes after rain.
safetyWarnings: Harvest only fresh white specimens — black inky stage is past prime.
Some people avoid all inky caps with alcohol.

matsutake.habitat: Under ponderosa pine and Douglas-fir — duff buried under needle litter. Eastern Oregon to Sierra.
matsutake.identification: White to brown cap with cottony veil remnants. Spicy cinnamon-cedar aroma when fresh. White gills. Stains brown when handled.
lookalikes: Deadly galerina — small brown on wood — TOXIC.
Catathelasma — larger, bitter, no matsutake aroma.
Amanita species — always excavate base and check for volva.
matsutake.edibleNotes: Highly prized in Japanese cuisine — aroma is the delicacy. Rice and clear broth showcase flavor.
matsutake.preparation: Gently clean — do not overwash aroma away. Slice and simmer in rice or soup.
matsutake.harvestSeason: Fall after first cools — September–November under pines.
safetyWarnings: High-stakes ID — go with experienced matsutake forager first seasons.
Never rake duff excessively — ecological and legal concerns on public land.

cauliflower-mushroom.habitat: Base of conifers — pine and fir roots. Often partially buried.
cauliflower-mushroom.identification: Large brain-like or noodle-like white-yellow mass of flattened branches. No cap. Grows from ground at tree base.
lookalikes: Rarely confused when full size — unique cauliflower form.
Some polypores at base — Sparassis is soft and fleshy.
cauliflower-mushroom.edibleNotes: Firm noodle texture — holds up in soups and stir-fries. Can weigh several pounds.
cauliflower-mushroom.preparation: Separate branches and wash out needles. Simmer or sauté until tender.
safetyWarnings: Clean thoroughly — traps forest debris.

candy-cap.habitat: Coastal oak-madrone and mixed hardwood duff — northern California specialty extending to Oregon coast.
candy-cap.identification: Small orange-brown lactarius with brittle flesh. Milky latex when cut. Dries to maple-syrup scent.
lookalikes: Other small orange lactarius — candy cap aroma when dried is definitive test.
Some russulas — no latex when cut.
candy-cap.edibleNotes: Famous for maple flavor when dried — cookies, ice cream, and syrup infusions.
candy-cap.preparation: Dry thoroughly to develop aroma. Grind into sugar for baking.
candy-cap.harvestSeason: Fall and winter — November–January on coast.
safetyWarnings: Confirm latex and maple scent when dried before culinary use.

saffron-milk-cap.habitat: Under pine — especially Monterey and ponderosa pine belts in southern Oregon and California mountains.
saffron-milk-cap.identification: Orange cap with darker concentric zones. Orange latex when cut. Brittle flesh. Green staining after handling.
lookalikes: Other orange lactarius — many require expert ID; saffron milk cap has carrot-orange latex.
False saffron milk caps — learn with mentor.
saffron-milk-cap.edibleNotes: Popular in Mediterranean cooking — grilled or pickled. Carrot-orange latex is key.
saffron-milk-cap.preparation: Cook thoroughly; traditional grilling over coals.
safetyWarnings: Lactarius ID is advanced — confirm latex color and pine association.

shrimp-russula.habitat: Conifer and mixed woods — often with hemlock and fir.
shrimp-russula.identification: Purple to wine-red cap fading with age. White gills. Stem bruises brown. Distinctive fish/shrimp odor when cooked.
lookalikes: Other russulas — many are toxic or acrid; shrimp russula is mild and fish-scented when cooked.
Never eat raw russula — taste test acridity only with expert guidance.
shrimp-russula.edibleNotes: One of the few reliably mild russulas when cooked — shrimp aroma develops in pan.
shrimp-russula.preparation: Cook thoroughly — never raw. Discard acrid specimens.
safetyWarnings: Russula group is for advanced foragers — learn shrimp russula with an expert.
Spit-test acridity only if trained.

prince-agaricus.habitat: Wood chip beds, roadsides, and forest edges — often near cedar and fir.
prince-agaricus.identification: Large brown-scaled cap, thick stem with skirt ring. Almond or anise scent. Gills pink then brown. Not yellow-staining.
lookalikes: Yellow-staining agaricus (A. xanthodermus) — phenolic smell, yellow bruising — GI illness.
Death angel (Amanita) — white gills when young, volva at base — DEADLY.
prince-agaricus.edibleNotes: Large meaty caps — almond aroma. Excellent grilled.
prince-agaricus.preparation: Cook until gills brown. Discard if yellow staining or phenolic smell.
safetyWarnings: Always check for yellow bruising at stem base and amanita volva when excavating.
Pink-then-brown gills, not white gills in mature specimen.

meadow-mushroom.habitat: Pastures, lawns, and grasslands after rain — not on wood.
meadow-mushroom.identification: White to brown cap, pink gills turning brown. Ring on stem. No yellow staining. Found in grass.
lookalikes: Destroying angel (Amanita) — white gills, volva, white cap — DEADLY in same habitat.
Yellow stainer — yellow bruising and phenolic odor.
meadow-mushroom.edibleNotes: Classic wild field mushroom — must be distinguished from amanita every time.
meadow-mushroom.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Only from grasslands with confirmed pink-brown gill progression.
meadow-mushroom.harvestSeason: Fall rains on open grass — September–November.
safetyWarnings: DEADLY amanita species grow in same lawns — dig entire base and check for volva.
Never eat with white gills.

pheasants-back.habitat: On dead hardwood logs and stumps — elm, maple, and cottonwood.
pheasants-back.identification: Large brown scaly cap resembling pheasant feathers. White porous underside. Grows on wood in spring.
lookalikes: Other polypores on wood — pheasant’s back has distinctive scaly cap pattern.
Not a gilled mushroom.
pheasants-back.edibleNotes: Only tender young margins edible — older tough. Watermelon-rind scent when fresh.
pheasants-back.preparation: Slice off soft outer inch and sauté. Make broth from older parts.
safetyWarnings: Older specimens are leathery — only eat young edges.

honey-mushroom.habitat: On wood and clustered at tree bases — pathogenic root rot fungus. Very common.
honey-mushroom.identification: Honey-brown cap in dense clusters on wood. Stem with black rhizomorphs. White spore print. Partial ring on stem.
lookalikes: Deadly galerina — smaller brown on wood — TOXIC — learn spore print and ring differences.
Jack-o-lantern — orange, gilled, bioluminescent.
honey-mushroom.edibleNotes: Edible when well-cooked — some people have sensitivity. Bulky harvests possible.
honey-mushroom.preparation: Boil or parboil 10+ minutes then sauté — never undercooked. Try small amount first time.
safetyWarnings: Must be well-cooked — raw or undercooked causes GI upset.
Some individuals allergic — first taste small portion.
Confirm not Galerina — deadly on same substrate.

blewit.habitat: Compost piles, leaf litter, and woody debris — often in rings.
blewit.identification: Lilac-purple cap and gills fading to tan. Spore print pinkish-buff. No ring on stem. Fruity floral smell.
lookalikes: Purple cortinarius — rusty spores and cortina web on young gills — TOXIC.
Other purple mushrooms — spore print and lack of cortina critical.
blewit.edibleNotes: Choice edible when purple — excellent flavor after cooking.
blewit.preparation: Cook thoroughly — do not eat raw. Beautiful in cream sauces.
blewit.harvestSeason: Late fall after first frosts — October–December.
safetyWarnings: Always spore print and rule out Cortinarius before eating.

wood-ear.habitat: On dead hardwood branches and logs — especially elder and maple.
wood-ear.identification: Rubbery ear-shaped brown translucent fruiting bodies. No gills. Cartilage texture.
lookalikes: Other jelly fungi — generally edible group; wood ear is most common culinary species.
wood-ear.edibleNotes: Classic Asian stir-fry ingredient — crunchy texture when rehydrated.
wood-ear.preparation: Dry and rehydrate, or simmer fresh in soup. Adds texture not flavor.
wood-ear.harvestSeason: Year-round on wood; peak after rains.
safetyWarnings: Only collect from clean wood away from roadside pollution.

enoki.habitat: On hardwood logs and stumps — especially elm and cottonwood in cool weather.
enoki.identification: Small orange caps with dark velvety stem base. Grows in cold weather on wood. Gilled.
lookalikes: Galerina on wood — DEADLY — always confirm spore print brown (enoki) vs. rusty brown (galerina) with expert.
Sulphur tuft — greenish gills, different season.
enoki.edibleNotes: Same species as cultivated enoki — wild form is shorter and more flavorful.
enoki.preparation: Cook in soups and hot pot. Harvest cool-season clusters.
enoki.harvestSeason: Late fall through winter on logs.
safetyWarnings: Wood-growing gilled mushrooms demand expert ID — high fatality risk if confused with Galerina.

slippery-jack.habitat: Under planted and wild pine — especially Scots and ponderosa pine plantations.
slippery-jack.identification: Brown cap with sticky slimy coating when wet. Yellow pores. Ring on stem. Grows with pines.
lookalikes: Other suillus — most edible when cap skin peeled; some bitter species.
Boletes — no ring typically; different pore attachment.
slippery-jack.edibleNotes: Edible after peeling slimy cap cuticle — mild flavor. Popular in Eastern Europe.
slippery-jack.preparation: Peel cap skin off before cooking. Pickle or sauté.
safetyWarnings: Always peel slimy cap — cuticle can cause GI upset for some.

wine-cap.habitat: Wood chip mulch, garden paths, and compost — urban and rural.
wine-cap.identification: Large burgundy wine-red cap fading to tan. Purple-gray gills. Thick ring on stem. Chips and compost habitat.
lookalikes: Other stropharia — wine cap is largest in mulch.
Agrocybe — different habitat and spore color.
wine-cap.edibleNotes: Excellent cultivated and wild mulch mushroom — asparagus-like when young.
wine-cap.preparation: Harvest before gills dark purple-black. Grill caps or sauté.
wine-cap.harvestSeason: Spring through fall on fresh wood chips.
safetyWarnings: Only from clean mulch — avoid treated or contaminated chips.

pig-ear-gomphus.habitat: Old-growth conifer duff — mountain hemlock and fir zones.
pig-ear-gomphus.identification: Clustered vase-shaped purple-brown caps with wrinkled undersurface (not gills). Fleshy.
lookalikes: Black trumpet — thinner, black, individual trumpets.
Some polypores — gomphus is fleshy violet-brown.
pig-ear-gomphus.edibleNotes: Historically eaten in PNW — some people report mild GI upset; try small portion first.
pig-ear-gomphus.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Used in traditional mountain foraging.
safetyWarnings: Can cause GI upset in sensitive individuals — taste small amount first.

pine-spike.habitat: Under pine — often near slippery jacks and boletes. Sandy pine duff.
pine-spike.identification: Orange-brown slimy cap, long slender stem. Grows with pines. Gilled (unusual for suillus associates).
lookalikes: Other chroogomphus — generally edible group under pine.
pine-spike.edibleNotes: Mild edible often collected alongside boletes — improves when dried.
pine-spike.preparation: Cook thoroughly; often added to mixed mushroom dishes.
safetyWarnings: Confirm pine habitat and gill structure.

combtooth.habitat: Hardwood logs — maple and oak wounds in valley and foothill forests.
combtooth.identification: Branched white icicle teeth — more coral-like than single lion’s mane. On hardwood.
lookalikes: Other Hericium — edible group.
combtooth.edibleNotes: Similar to lion’s mane — choice edible on hardwood.
safetyWarnings: Fresh white only.

charcoal-burner.identification: Green to purple cap. White gills that do not shatter when rolled between fingers (flexible gills — key trait).
lookalikes: Other russulas — most have brittle gills; flexible gills distinguish this edible species.
Acidic russulas — taste acrid raw (spit test only if trained).
charcoal-burner.edibleNotes: One of the few non-acrid russulas — flexible gill test is diagnostic.
charcoal-burner.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Popular in European foraging tradition.
safetyWarnings: Russula group — confirm flexible gills and mild taste with expert.

black-morel.habitat: Burn scars, riparian cottonwoods, and disturbed ground in mountains — spring.
black-morel.identification: Dark brown elongated honeycombed cap. Completely hollow stem and cap. Pits and ridges (not wrinkled brain-like).
lookalikes: False morel (Gyromitra) — brain-like RED-BROWN cap, NOT fully hollow — TOXIC.
Verpa — cap attached only at apex of stem.
black-morel.edibleNotes: Mountain burn morel — highly prized spring harvest in Sierra and Cascades.
black-morel.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Split and wash. Never raw.
black-morel.harvestSeason: Spring — April–June at elevation, especially year after fire.
safetyWarnings: Must be completely hollow inside — false morels are solid or chambered.

california-chanterelle.habitat: Under oaks in Sierra foothills and interior valleys — large golden clusters in leaf litter.
california-chanterelle.identification: Very large golden chanterelle with false forked ridges. Strong apricot scent. Often grows in massive clumps under live oak.
lookalikes: Pacific golden chanterelle — smaller, more conifer-associated.
Jack-o-lantern (Omphalotus) — true gills, grows on wood — TOXIC.
california-chanterelle.edibleNotes: One of the largest chanterelles in North America — excellent dried or sautéed.
california-chanterelle.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Slice thick caps; dry excess.
california-chanterelle.harvestSeason: Fall through early winter after rains — October–December.
safetyWarnings: Confirm false gills and apricot scent.

blue-chanterelle.habitat: Old-growth conifer forests — mossy ground under spruce and fir at higher elevation.
blue-chanterelle.identification: Dark blue-black to purple clustered fan-shaped caps with wrinkled undersides (not true gills). Grows in tight groups.
lookalikes: Black trumpet — single trumpet shape, not clustered fans.
Any gilled mushroom — blue chanterelle has ridges/wrinkles only.
blue-chanterelle.edibleNotes: Choice edible with earthy flavor — popular in PNW high-country foraging.
blue-chanterelle.harvestSeason: Late summer through fall at elevation.
safetyWarnings: Verify wrinkled underside — no true gills.

queen-bolete.habitat: Under oaks and mixed hardwoods — Sierra foothills and coastal oak woodlands.
queen-bolete.identification: Large brown cap, thick reticulated stem, white pores that age yellow-green. Nutty aroma. Does not stain blue.
lookalikes: King bolete — more conifer-associated; both choice edibles.
Bitter bolete (Caloboletus) — stains blue, bitter taste.
queen-bolete.edibleNotes: Premier NorCal oak bolete — often called the queen to the king porcini.
queen-bolete.preparation: Grill caps, dry slices, or sauté in butter.
safetyWarnings: Spore print olive-brown. No blue staining.

butter-bolete.habitat: Under ponderosa pine and mixed conifers in mountains and east-side forests.
butter-bolete.identification: Red-brown cap, yellow pores, stout yellow stem often with red mesh. Buttery aroma when young.
lookalikes: King bolete — similar; both edible. Bitter bolete — blue stains.
butter-bolete.edibleNotes: Excellent pine-associated bolete in eastern Cascades and Sierra.
butter-bolete.preparation: Young firm specimens sautéed; remove spongy pores if desired.
safetyWarnings: Confirm non-bitter taste and no blue staining.

bay-bolete.habitat: Conifer and mixed woods — often with spruce and fir on coast.
bay-bolete.identification: Bay-brown cap, yellow pores that bruise blue-green, yellow stem with brown reticulation. Flesh may blue slightly.
lookalikes: Bitter bolete — intensely bitter; bay bolete is mild.
King bolete — larger, paler pore surface when young.
bay-bolete.edibleNotes: Good edible — peel slimy cap cuticle before cooking. Mild flavor.
bay-bolete.preparation: Peel cap skin; cook thoroughly. Remove blue-stained pore layer if desired.
safetyWarnings: Blue bruising is normal — do not confuse with toxic boletes.

cracked-cap-bolete.habitat: Urban parks, lawns, and mixed woods — very common small bolete.
cracked-cap-bolete.identification: Small brown cap cracking to show red flesh underneath. Yellow pores age reddish. Stem often reddish at base.
lookalikes: Other small boletes — generally edible if mild taste.
cracked-cap-bolete.edibleNotes: Common edible — best when young and firm. Can be buggy at maturity.
cracked-cap-bolete.preparation: Cook young specimens; discard soft or wormy ones.
safetyWarnings: Small size — verify pore surface not gills.

aspen-bolete.habitat: Under aspen and cottonwood in eastern Oregon and Modoc Plateau.
aspen-bolete.identification: Brown cap with dark scabers (dots) on white to gray stem. White flesh. Grows with poplar relatives.
lookalikes: Other Leccinum — most require thorough cooking; some cause GI upset if undercooked.
Orange-capped scaber stalk — different cap color.
aspen-bolete.edibleNotes: Edible when well-cooked — leccinums need longer cooking than other boletes.
aspen-bolete.preparation: Cook at least 15–20 minutes. Do not eat raw or lightly sautéed.
safetyWarnings: ALWAYS cook leccinums thoroughly — undercooking causes nausea for some people.

manzanita-bolete.habitat: Under manzanita and madrone in chaparral-woodland edges.
manzanita-bolete.identification: Brown to gray cap, stem with dark scabers, often stocky. Found only near manzanita hosts.
lookalikes: Other Leccinum — cook thoroughly.
manzanita-bolete.edibleNotes: Regional specialty — good when thoroughly cooked.
manzanita-bolete.preparation: Extended cooking required — soups or stews ideal.
safetyWarnings: Cook leccinums thoroughly — never raw.

conifer-chicken.habitat: Parasitic on living and dead conifers — shelf clusters on trunks.
conifer-chicken.identification: Bright orange to salmon shelving brackets with yellow pore underside. Soft when young. On conifers (not hardwood).
lookalikes: Hardwood chicken (Laetiporus gilbertsonii) — on oak/madrone in California.
Jack-o-lantern — gilled, grows in clusters on wood — TOXIC.
conifer-chicken.edibleNotes: Choice when young and tender — some people react to conifer species; try small amount first.
conifer-chicken.preparation: Harvest outer 2 inches only. Cook thoroughly. Not everyone tolerates conifer chicken.
safetyWarnings: Eat a small cooked portion first time — rare allergic reactions reported.
Never eat raw.

early-morel.habitat: Mulched landscaping, disturbed soil, wood chips — urban and suburban spring flushes.
early-morel.identification: Small tan to brown conical morel. Bruises reddish-brown. Honeycombed cap fully attached to stem. Hollow inside.
lookalikes: False morel (Gyromitra) — brain-like, not fully hollow — TOXIC.
Verpa — cap hangs free from stem apex.
early-morel.edibleNotes: First morel of the season in cities — reliable in wood-chip beds.
early-morel.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Wash grit from honeycomb.
safetyWarnings: Must be completely hollow. Avoid contaminated urban sites.

half-free-morel.habitat: Hardwood edges, riparian zones, and disturbed ground in spring.
half-free-morel.identification: Cap attached only at apex of stem (half-free). Honeycombed brown cap. Completely hollow stem and cap.
lookalikes: Verpa bohemica — cap hangs like a thimble; stem stuffed with cottony tissue — not recommended.
False morel — not hollow.
half-free-morel.edibleNotes: Good edible — less prized than yellow or black morels but abundant.
half-free-morel.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Split and clean hollow stem.
safetyWarnings: Confirm hollow interior and honeycomb (not brain-like) cap.

yellow-morel.habitat: Cottonwood riparian zones, old orchards, ash and elm associations in valleys.
yellow-morel.identification: Tan to yellow honeycombed cap fully attached to white hollow stem. Entire mushroom hollow when cut.
lookalikes: False morel — solid or chambered interior — TOXIC.
yellow-morel.edibleNotes: Classic spring delicacy — among the most sought-after wild mushrooms.
yellow-morel.preparation: Sauté in butter; stuff; never eat raw.
yellow-morel.harvestSeason: Spring — March through May in valleys.
safetyWarnings: Must be completely hollow inside.

crown-coral.habitat: Dead hardwood logs and stumps — common on alder and maple.
crown-coral.identification: White to cream branching coral with crown-like depressed tips. Grows on wood. No gelatinous base.
lookalikes: Other corals — some Ramaria; verify crown-shaped tips.
White spindle coral on ground — different growth habit.
crown-coral.edibleNotes: Tender when young — mild flavor. Harvest before tips brown.
crown-coral.preparation: Sauté young white clusters; bitter when old.
crown-coral.harvestSeason: Summer through fall on rotting hardwood.
safetyWarnings: Only on wood. Avoid any coral you cannot ID to species.

golden-coral.habitat: Conifer forest floor — often near spruce and fir.
golden-coral.identification: Bright golden-yellow branching coral, tips often pointed. White spore print. Grows from soil not wood.
lookalikes: Other Ramaria — some cause GI upset; golden coral is a safe edible group when identified correctly.
Yellow-tipped coral — similar; expert ID recommended.
golden-coral.edibleNotes: Choice coral mushroom — breaks easily, cooks like cauliflower.
golden-coral.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Discard any with bitter taste.
safetyWarnings: Coral mushrooms require careful ID — start with known golden coral.

orange-peel-fungus.habitat: Compacted soil, gravel roadsides, trail edges — often in groups.
orange-peel-fungus.identification: Bright orange cup-shaped fungus that looks like scattered orange peels. No stem. Smooth outer surface.
lookalikes: Scarlet cup — brighter red, on wood.
Any cup fungus — orange peel is distinctive on bare soil.
orange-peel-fungus.edibleNotes: Edible but bland — more a curiosity than a meal.
safetyWarnings: Avoid roadside specimens with contamination.

fried-chicken-mushroom.habitat: Grass, mulch, and compacted soil — urban parks and landscaped areas.
fried-chicken-mushroom.identification: Tan-brown caps in tight clusters, white gills, white spore print. Smooth cap without scales.
lookalikes: Deadly Galerina — brown spore print, ring on stem — TOXIC.
Honey mushroom — ring and spore print differ.
fried-chicken-mushroom.edibleNotes: Good urban edible when spore print confirmed white.
fried-chicken-mushroom.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Confirm white spore print.
fried-chicken-mushroom.harvestSeason: Fall through spring in mild climates.
safetyWarnings: WHITE spore print essential — deadly lookalikes have brown spores.

brick-cap.habitat: Clusters on dead hardwood logs and stumps — especially maple and alder.
brick-cap.identification: Brick-red cap with yellowish margin when young. Grows in overlapping clusters on wood. Purple-brown spore print.
lookalikes: Sulfur tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) — greenish-yellow gills, bitter — TOXIC.
Must compare gill color — brick cap has gray-brown gills.
brick-cap.edibleNotes: Edible when young — sulfur tuft is the dangerous lookalike on same substrate.
brick-cap.preparation: Harvest young caps; cook thoroughly. Avoid sulfur-tuft lookalikes.
brick-cap.harvestSeason: Fall through winter on rotting logs.
safetyWarnings: NEVER confuse with sulfur tuft — verify gray-brown gills not green-yellow.

shingled-hedgehog.habitat: Under conifers — especially pine and spruce in mountains.
shingled-hedgehog.identification: Large brown cap with dark scaly shingles. Underside has teeth (spines) not gills. Often bitter when old.
lookalikes: Hedgehog mushroom — smoother cap, not scaly.
Old specimens become too bitter to eat.
shingled-hedgehog.edibleNotes: Edible when young — choose firm specimens with mild flavor.
shingled-hedgehog.preparation: Young caps only; older ones are bitter. Long cooking helps.
shingled-hedgehog.harvestSeason: Late summer through fall at elevation.
safetyWarnings: Spines not gills — verify tooth underside.

terracotta-hedgehog.habitat: Conifer and mixed forest floor — often near moss and spruce.
terracotta-hedgehog.identification: Small orange-tan cap with white to pale spines underneath. Compact stature. Spines descend stem slightly.
lookalikes: Sweet tooth hedgehog — larger, paler; both edible.
terracotta-hedgehog.edibleNotes: Choice small hedgehog — excellent flavor relative to size.
safetyWarnings: Confirm spines — not gills.

pear-shaped-puffball.habitat: Clusters on rotting logs and stumps — extremely common.
pear-shaped-puffball.identification: Small pear-shaped brownish puffballs growing in dense clusters on wood. White interior when young.
lookalikes: Earthballs (Scleroderma) — interior dark from youth — TOXIC.
Must be pure white inside.
pear-shaped-puffball.edibleNotes: Good when young and white throughout — peel outer skin.
pear-shaped-puffball.preparation: Slice and sauté only pure white interior.
safetyWarnings: Cut every puffball in half — pure white only.

horse-mushroom.habitat: Pastures, meadows, and grassy areas — often in fairy rings.
horse-mushroom.identification: Large white cap staining yellow. Ring on stem. Pink gills aging brown. Anise or almond scent.
lookalikes: Destroying angel (Amanita) — volva at base, white gills — DEADLY.
Yellow stainer — intense yellow stain, phenolic smell — causes GI illness.
horse-mushroom.edibleNotes: Excellent meadow mushroom when Amanita ruled out (no volva, brown spores).
horse-mushroom.preparation: Cook thoroughly. Dig stem base to check for volva.
safetyWarnings: Check for volva at stem base — Amanita is deadly.

poplar-mushroom.habitat: Cottonwood and poplar stumps and buried wood in riparian zones.
poplar-mushroom.identification: Brown cap, white stem with ring, gills aging brown. Grows in clusters on poplar wood.
lookalikes: Galerina — brown spores on wood; always take spore print.
poplar-mushroom.edibleNotes: Cultivated worldwide — wild on cottonwood in valley riparian zones.
poplar-mushroom.preparation: Sauté stems and caps — stems are tender.
safetyWarnings: On wood — rule out Galerina with spore print.

elm-oyster.habitat: Wounds on living hardwoods — elm, cottonwood, and maple in riparian areas.
elm-oyster.identification: Tan cap, white gills, stem attached to wood. Often high on tree trunks. White spore print.
lookalikes: Oyster mushroom — grows from stumps lower; both edible.
elm-oyster.edibleNotes: Mild firm texture — good stir-fry mushroom.
safetyWarnings: On hardwood wounds — white spore print.

man-on-horseback.habitat: Under pine and fir — sandy duff in coastal and montane forests.
man-on-horseback.identification: White to brown cap, white gills, thick white stem with cottony ring. Strong cinnamon-spice aroma.
lookalikes: Matsutake (Tricholoma magnivelare) — closely related; both prized.
Amanita — volva at base; matsutake has no volva.
man-on-horseback.edibleNotes: Prized for aroma — used in rice and soups. Related to Japanese matsutake.
man-on-horseback.preparation: Brush clean; do not wash. Cook in rice or clear soup.
safetyWarnings: Dig base to confirm no volva (Amanita).

painted-suillus.identification: Brown cap with reddish pattern, yellow pores, ring on stem. Slimy cap when wet.
lookalikes: Other Suillus — generally edible with peeling cap cuticle.
painted-suillus.edibleNotes: Edible when cap skin peeled — mucilaginous cap is unpalatable otherwise.
painted-suillus.preparation: Peel slimy cap cuticle; cook thoroughly.
safetyWarnings: Always peel cap skin on suillus species.

larch-bolete.habitat: Exclusively under larch (tamarack) in subalpine zones.
larch-bolete.identification: Yellow to orange slimy cap, yellow pores, yellow stem with dark dots. Grows only with larch.
lookalikes: Other Suillus — peel cap; host tree is diagnostic.
larch-bolete.edibleNotes: Good when young with peeled cap — larch host is key ID feature.
larch-bolete.harvestSeason: Late summer through fall at elevation.
safetyWarnings: Confirm larch host tree present.

amethyst-deceiver.habitat: Mossy conifer forest floor — common and widespread.
amethyst-deceiver.identification: Small purple to amethyst cap fading with age. Thick purple gills. White spore print. Fibrous stem.
lookalikes: Other Laccaria — generally edible group.
Purple cortinarius — rusty spore print; spore print essential.
amethyst-deceiver.edibleNotes: Small but abundant — good in mixed mushroom medleys.
safetyWarnings: Take spore print — Cortinarius has rusty brown spores.

common-deceiver.habitat: Virtually all forest types — one of the most common forest floor mushrooms.
common-deceiver.identification: Small tawny to orange-brown cap, thick widely spaced gills, fibrous stem. White spore print.
lookalikes: Other small brown mushrooms — spore print white for Laccaria.
common-deceiver.edibleNotes: Abundant and edible — small size makes it best in mixes.
common-deceiver.preparation: Cook in stews or mixed sauté.
common-deceiver.harvestSeason: Year-round in mild coastal forests; peak fall.
safetyWarnings: White spore print — rule out Cortinarius.

white-elfin-saddle.habitat: Hardwood and mixed forest edges — often near paths in sandy soil.
white-elfin-saddle.identification: White convoluted saddle-shaped cap on white ribbed stem. No gills — cap is folded and brain-like.
lookalikes: Other Helvella — most edible cooked; H. vespertina is darker.
False morel — different shape and season.
white-elfin-saddle.edibleNotes: Edible when cooked — contains heat-labile toxins; never raw.
white-elfin-saddle.preparation: MUST be cooked thoroughly — parboil then sauté. Never eat raw.
safetyWarnings: RAW HELVELLA IS TOXIC — cook thoroughly every time.

western-elfin-saddle.habitat: Under conifers — especially pine and fir on NorCal coast.
western-elfin-saddle.identification: Dark gray-brown convoluted saddle cap on pale ribbed stem. Larger than white elfin saddle.
lookalikes: False morel — different cap attachment and interior.
western-elfin-saddle.edibleNotes: Edible cooked — popular NorCal spring mushroom when prepared correctly.
western-elfin-saddle.preparation: Parboil 5 minutes, discard water, then sauté. Never raw.
safetyWarnings: Must be parboiled and cooked — raw helvellas are toxic.

ruby-bolete.habitat: Urban parks, lawns, and oak woodlands — often in groups.
ruby-bolete.identification: Small red cap, yellow pores, slender red stem. Blue stains quickly when cut. Mild taste.
lookalikes: Red-pored bolete — red pores indicate bitter/toxic; ruby has yellow pores.
Small size distinguishes from larger boletes.
ruby-bolete.edibleNotes: Small but good — mild flavor when young.
safetyWarnings: Yellow pores only — red pores mean do not eat.
